vectors: Compromised remote fleet-management platform credential
Exploited vulnerability in the fleet-management software or its update mechanism
Supply-chain compromise of the remote management vendor
rootCauses: Unpatched remote management software
Lack of MFA on fleet-management platform accounts
Insufficient network segmentation between the fleet-management platform and billboard hardware
controls: MFA on fleet-management platform accounts
Network segmentation between fleet-management systems and billboard hardware
Patch management for remote management software
ITID-21613.detection: Fleet-management platform audit logs and cross-site correlation of simultaneous defacements provide the primary detection signal.
ITID-21613.response: Isolate the fleet-management platform, rotate credentials, and audit all billboards in the fleet for unauthorized content or firmware changes.
metrics: Number of billboards affected per incident
Time to isolate the compromised fleet-management platform
ITID-21613.notes: Differentiated from ITID-21611 by targeting the dedicated device/fleet-management layer rather than the ad-serving/scheduling CMS, and from ITID-21612 by being a remote rather than physical access vector.

playbook.name: Response: Digital Billboard Defacement via Compromised Remote Management Software
playbook.description: For a digital billboard defaced through compromise of the remote management/monitoring software used to control it over the network.

steps.title: Capture the unauthorized content and confirm the remote-management pathway
steps.desc: Photograph/record the unauthorized display and confirm the content was pushed via the remote management software rather than physical access.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized content documented; remote-management pathway confirmed.

steps.title: Disconnect the billboard from the remote management network or pull it offline
steps.desc: Immediately stop further unauthorized pushes by isolating the display from the compromised management channel.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized content no longer displaying; display isolated.

steps.title: Patch or update the remote management software
steps.desc: Apply any available patch and close the specific vulnerability or exposure identified during identification.

steps.title: Reconnect and restore the approved creative content
steps.desc: Reconnect the display once the software is patched and secured, and confirm it shows only approved content.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend network exposure reduction, patch cadence, and credential hygiene for remote-management platforms.

steps.title: Determine how the remote management software was compromised
steps.desc: Review the software's access logs and network exposure to determine whether it was compromised via stolen credentials, an exposed management port, or a vulnerable version.
steps.guidance: Remote billboard/signage management software is frequently exposed to the internet with default or weak credentials — check this first.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by disconnecting the display from the management network.

steps.title: Rotate remote-management credentials and restrict network exposure
steps.desc: Reset all credentials for the management software and restrict its network access (e.g. VPN-only, IP allowlist) if it was internet-exposed.

steps.title: Check all other displays managed by the same platform for tampering
steps.desc: A compromised remote management platform can typically reach every connected display, not just the one first noticed.

ITID-21614.def: Defacement of a company digital billboard, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (compromised ad-network/CMS, physical/local access, or compromised remote management software).
ITID-21614.purpose: Catch-all for digital billboard defacement cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific billboard-defacement leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-21611 through ITID-21613)
ITID-21614.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High pending clarification given billboard public visibility.
ITID-21614.escalation: Reclassify once the specific access vector is clarified.
indicators: Report of defaced billboard content with unclear access vector
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Digital signage management console MFA enforcement
Network segmentation for signage control systems
Scheduled content-integrity verification
ITID-21614.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-21614.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-21614.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Digital Billboard Defacement
playbook.description: Catch-all response for digital billboard content tampering that does not clearly fit the ad-network/CMS-compromise, physical-console-access, or remote-management-compromise categories.

steps.title: Capture the unauthorized content and determine the delivery pathway
steps.desc: Photograph/record the unauthorized display and determine whether it was delivered remotely or via physical access.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized content documented; delivery pathway identified.

steps.title: Pull the billboard offline or switch to a default/safe creative
steps.desc: Stop the unauthorized content from displaying by whatever means available (vendor console, physical shutdown).

steps.title: Close the exploited access vector
steps.desc: Address the compromised credential, vulnerability, or physical-security gap identified during identification.

steps.title: Restore the approved creative content
steps.desc: Confirm the billboard is displaying only approved, verified content.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and one concrete improvement, and note whether a more specific ITID category should have been used.

steps.title: Determine the access vector used
steps.desc: Review whichever system (ad network, CMS, remote management, or physical logs) is relevant to determine how access was gained.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by pulling the billboard offline.

steps.title: Rotate relevant credentials and secure physical access if applicable
steps.desc: Reset relevant credentials, and coordinate with Facilities/Physical Security if physical access may have been involved.
steps.outcome: Old credentials invalidated; physical access secured if relevant.

steps.title: Coordinate a public statement with PR/Comms if the display was widely seen
steps.desc: Assess whether a public acknowledgment is warranted given the public-facing nature of a billboard.

ITID-21621.def: Unauthorized alteration of content displayed on lobby or reception-area digital signage.
ITID-21621.purpose: Captures defacement of digital signage in a company lobby or reception area, the first physical brand touchpoint for visitors.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized content displayed on a lobby welcome screen or visitor directory display
Tampering with reception-area digital signage content
scopeExcludes: Defacement of meeting room/conference room displays (ITID-21622)
Defacement achieved specifically via a compromised signage CMS (ITID-21623) or a rogue HDMI/casting device (ITID-21624) as the differentiating access vector
ITID-21621.severity: Medium; visible to visitors and employees at a single site, generally lower reach than a public billboard.
ITID-21621.priority: P3, escalating to P2 if the content is offensive or if visitors/clients witness it directly.
ITID-21621.escalation: Escalate to IT security and facilities/front-desk staff to restore the display promptly.
indicators: Front-desk staff or visitor reports of unusual lobby signage content
Signage management system showing unauthorized content push
vectors: Compromised signage management account
Physical tampering with the lobby display's input source
rootCauses: Weak access controls on the signage management system
Unsecured signage hardware inputs in a publicly accessible lobby
controls: Access controls on signage management accounts
Physical securing of lobby display input ports
ITID-21621.detection: Front-desk/facilities staff observation is typically the first signal; signage management logs corroborate the technical cause.
ITID-21621.response: Restore approved content promptly and secure the input source or account used.
metrics: Time to restore lobby signage content
ITID-21621.notes: Scoped to lobby/reception signage location specifically; access-vector siblings (signage CMS, rogue HDMI/casting device) carry the underlying-cause detail.

playbook.name: Response: Lobby/Reception Digital Signage Defacement
playbook.description: For unauthorized or offensive content displayed on lobby/reception digital signage, a high-visibility on-site display seen by visitors, candidates, and clients.

steps.title: Immediately alert on-site facilities/reception staff and document the display
steps.desc: Given visitors and clients see this display directly, notify reception/facilities staff right away so they can manage the immediate visitor-facing impact while photographing the unauthorized content for the record.
steps.outcome: On-site staff aware; unauthorized content documented.

steps.title: Power off or disconnect the display immediately
steps.desc: Stop the unauthorized content from being visible to visitors as quickly as possible, even if that means simply unplugging the display.

steps.title: Close the exploited access vector
steps.desc: Address the compromised credential, vulnerability, or physical-security gap identified during identification.

steps.title: Restore the approved content and reconnect the display
steps.desc: Confirm the display shows only approved content before reconnecting it for visitor visibility.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend a hardening improvement, coordinating with Facilities on physical-access controls if relevant.

steps.title: Determine whether the cause is remote (signage CMS) or physical (on-site access)
steps.desc: Check the signage CMS/remote-management logs first, and check for signs of physical tampering (rogue HDMI/USB device, console access) if remote logs show nothing.
steps.outcome: Access vector — remote or physical — identified.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by powering off the display.

steps.title: Rotate signage CMS credentials and/or secure physical access
steps.desc: Reset CMS credentials and, if physical access was involved, coordinate with Facilities/Physical Security to secure the area.
steps.outcome: Old credentials invalidated and/or physical access secured.

ITID-21622.def: Unauthorized alteration of content displayed on a meeting room or conference room screen.
ITID-21622.purpose: Captures defacement of a meeting room or conference room display, typically used for presentations and video conferencing.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized content appearing on a meeting room display during or between meetings
Tampering with the conference room display's default/idle screen content
scopeExcludes: Defacement of lobby/reception signage (ITID-21621)
Defacement achieved specifically via a compromised signage CMS (ITID-21623) or a rogue HDMI/casting device (ITID-21624) as the differentiating access vector
ITID-21622.severity: Low-Medium; typically visible only to employees/meeting participants in a single room, with limited external reach.
ITID-21622.priority: P3, escalating to P2 if the content appears during a client-facing meeting or video conference.
ITID-21622.escalation: Escalate to IT/facilities to restore the display; escalate further if a client witnessed the defacement during a call.
indicators: Employee/meeting-participant reports of unusual display content
Conference room AV system logs showing an unauthorized input or content source
vectors: Rogue device connected to the room's AV input
Compromised room-booking/AV management system
rootCauses: Unsecured AV input ports in shared meeting rooms
Lack of monitoring on room AV management systems
controls: Physical securing/monitoring of meeting room AV input ports
Access controls on room AV/booking management systems
ITID-21622.detection: Employee/participant reports are typically the first signal; AV system logs corroborate the technical cause where available.
ITID-21622.response: Restore the default/approved content and inspect the room's AV inputs for unauthorized devices.
metrics: Time to restore meeting room display content
ITID-21622.notes: Scoped to meeting/conference room location specifically; access-vector siblings (signage CMS, rogue HDMI/casting device) carry the underlying-cause detail.

playbook.name: Response: Meeting Room/Conference Display Defacement
playbook.description: For unauthorized or offensive content displayed on a meeting room/conference room display, potentially disrupting or embarrassing a meeting with clients or partners present.

steps.title: Disconnect the display and document the incident
steps.desc: If a meeting is in progress, immediately disconnect/power off the display to limit embarrassment, then document what was shown.

steps.title: Remove any rogue device and disable open casting/wireless-display access
steps.desc: Physically remove any unauthorized device and disable open Wi-Fi casting to the display until secured.
steps.outcome: Rogue access removed; casting access controlled.

steps.title: Secure the casting/AV configuration against unauthenticated connections
steps.desc: Require authentication or pairing codes for casting to the display going forward.

steps.title: Restore normal display operation and verify
steps.desc: Confirm the display functions normally and shows only intended content before the room is used again.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend securing casting access across meeting rooms company-wide.

steps.title: Determine whether the cause is a rogue casting/HDMI device or a compromised signage/AV system
steps.desc: Check the room for an unfamiliar device connected to the display (rogue HDMI dongle, casting device) and check AV/signage system logs if the room uses managed AV.
steps.guidance: Meeting room displays are especially prone to opportunistic physical tampering via wireless casting or an unattended HDMI port.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by removing/disabling any casting capability.

steps.title: Rotate any AV/signage system credentials if a managed system was involved
steps.desc: Reset credentials for any managed AV/signage platform found to be compromised.

steps.title: Follow up with any external attendees if the incident occurred during a client/partner meeting
steps.desc: If clients or partners witnessed the incident, coordinate a brief, professional follow-up with the relevant account owner.
steps.outcome: External relationship impact addressed if needed.

ITID-21623.def: Unauthorized alteration of office digital signage content achieved by compromising the signage CMS that centrally manages and pushes content to multiple displays across one or more locations.
ITID-21623.purpose: Captures office display defacement achieved through compromise of the centralized signage content-management system controlling multiple displays.
scopeIncludes: Compromised signage CMS admin account used to push unauthorized content fleet-wide
Exploited vulnerability in the signage CMS platform
scopeExcludes: Defacement via a rogue physical HDMI/casting device connected directly to a single display (ITID-21624)
Defacement confined to a single display without evidence of centralized CMS compromise (ITID-21621/21622)
ITID-21623.severity: Medium-High; CMS-level compromise can affect multiple displays across multiple office locations simultaneously.
ITID-21623.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if multiple sites/displays are affected simultaneously.
ITID-21623.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security to lock down the signage CMS and prevent further unauthorized pushes.
indicators: Signage CMS admin console showing unauthorized content pushes
Multiple displays across different rooms/sites showing the same unauthorized content simultaneously
vectors: Compromised signage CMS admin credential
Exploited vulnerability in the signage CMS platform
rootCauses: Lack of MFA on signage CMS admin accounts
Unpatched signage CMS software
controls: MFA on signage CMS admin accounts
Patch management for the signage CMS platform
ITID-21623.detection: Signage CMS audit logs and cross-site correlation of simultaneous defacements provide the primary detection signal.
ITID-21623.response: Lock down the signage CMS, rotate admin credentials, and push approved content back to all affected displays.
metrics: Number of displays/sites affected per incident
Time to lock down the compromised CMS
ITID-21623.notes: Differentiated from ITID-21624 by the remote/centralized CMS access vector rather than a local physical device.

playbook.name: Response: Office Display Defacement via Compromised Signage CMS
playbook.description: For office digital signage (lobby, meeting room, break room, etc.) displaying unauthorized content due to compromise of the central signage content-management platform.

steps.title: Document the unauthorized content and identify all affected displays
steps.desc: Photograph the unauthorized content and check the signage CMS to identify every display/screen group it was pushed to — a CMS compromise often affects multiple displays at once.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized content documented; full scope of affected displays identified.

steps.title: Push a default/safe screen or disconnect all affected displays
steps.desc: Immediately stop unauthorized content from displaying across every affected screen.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized content no longer displaying anywhere.

steps.title: Patch or close the exploited vulnerability in the signage CMS
steps.desc: Update the CMS version or close the misconfiguration/exposed interface identified during identification.

steps.title: Restore approved content across all affected displays
steps.desc: Confirm every affected display is back to showing only approved content.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and one concrete improvement (patch cadence, credential hygiene, MFA on the CMS).

steps.title: Determine how the signage CMS was compromised
steps.desc: Review the CMS's audit logs to determine whether the compromise came from a stolen admin credential, a vulnerable CMS version, or an exposed management interface.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by disconnecting all displays from the CMS.

steps.title: Rotate signage CMS credentials for all admin/editor accounts
steps.desc: Reset passwords and API keys for every account with content-publishing access to the CMS.

ITID-21624.def: Unauthorized alteration of office digital signage or meeting-room display content achieved by physically attaching a rogue HDMI input source or unauthorized wireless casting/streaming device.
ITID-21624.purpose: Captures office display defacement achieved by physically connecting a rogue HDMI source or unauthorized casting/streaming device to a display.
scopeIncludes: Rogue HDMI device or laptop plugged into a display's input to show unauthorized content
Unauthorized wireless casting device (e.g. rogue Chromecast/streaming stick) used to push content to a display
scopeExcludes: Defacement via a compromised centralized signage CMS (ITID-21623)
Legitimate employee use of a casting device for an approved presentation (not a security incident)
ITID-21624.severity: Low-Medium; requires physical proximity, limiting scale, but is trivial to execute if input ports/casting are unsecured.
ITID-21624.priority: P3, escalating to P2 if repeated or if it occurs during a client-facing setting.
ITID-21624.escalation: Escalate to facilities/physical security to identify who connected the rogue device; escalate to IT security if the device shows signs of being used for a broader intrusion attempt.
indicators: Unrecognized device found connected to a display's HDMI/input port
Display suddenly showing content from an unrecognized wireless casting source
Employee report of unusual content appearing when entering a room
vectors: Physically accessible, unsecured HDMI/input ports on office displays
Unsecured or default-open wireless casting receivers
rootCauses: Lack of physical port security (e.g. port locks/covers) on office displays
Wireless casting receivers left in an open/unauthenticated pairing mode
controls: Physical port locks/covers on office display inputs
Authentication/pairing requirements on wireless casting receivers
ITID-21624.detection: Primarily physical observation (employee/facilities report); some casting systems log connection events which can corroborate.
ITID-21624.response: Remove the rogue device, restore the intended content source, and review physical/wireless access controls for the room.
metrics: Count of rogue-device display incidents per site per year
detections: Wireless casting receiver connection logging (where available)
ITID-21624.notes: Differentiated from ITID-21623 by the local physical/wireless hardware access vector rather than a remote centralized CMS compromise; no real network vector typically exists here beyond the local pairing, so techniques are limited accordingly.

playbook.name: Response: Office Display Defacement via Rogue HDMI/Casting Device
playbook.description: For an office digital display defaced by an attacker physically connecting a rogue HDMI or wireless casting device to inject unauthorized content.

steps.title: Locate and photograph the rogue device before removing it
steps.desc: Identify the unauthorized HDMI dongle, streaming stick, or casting device connected to the display and photograph it in place as evidence before disconnecting.
steps.guidance: This is fundamentally a physical security incident — loop in Facilities/Physical Security immediately.

steps.title: Remove the rogue device and power-cycle the display
steps.desc: Disconnect the unauthorized device and restore the display to its normal input source.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized content stopped; display restored to normal source.

steps.title: Inspect for any additional rogue devices in nearby displays
steps.desc: Check other displays in the same area/building for similar tampering.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional rogue devices found and removed.

steps.title: Verify normal display operation
steps.desc: Confirm the display is functioning normally and showing only intended content.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend physical-security hardening
steps.desc: Record how physical access was gained and recommend port security, camera coverage, or badge-access improvements at the site.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and shared with Facilities/Physical Security.

steps.title: Review physical access logs/CCTV for the area and time window
steps.desc: Determine who had physical access to the display's location during the relevant window.
steps.outcome: Access window and, where possible, the individual(s) responsible identified.
steps.abort: If access cannot be attributed, treat as an unknown-actor physical intrusion and proceed to containment.

steps.title: Secure physical access to the display's ports and location
steps.desc: Where feasible, restrict physical access to the display's HDMI/USB ports (locking cabinet, port blockers) to prevent recurrence.

ITID-21625.def: Defacement of an office digital display, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (lobby/reception, meeting room, compromised signage CMS, or rogue HDMI/casting device).
ITID-21625.purpose: Catch-all for office display defacement cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific office-display leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-21621 through ITID-21624)
ITID-21625.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Low-Medium pending clarification.
ITID-21625.escalation: Reclassify once the specific display location and access vector are clarified.
indicators: Report of defaced office display content with unclear location or vector
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Office display management console MFA enforcement
Network segmentation for display control systems
Scheduled content-integrity verification
ITID-21625.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-21625.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-21625.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Office Display Defacement
playbook.description: Catch-all response for office digital display tampering that does not clearly fit the lobby-signage, meeting-room-display, signage-CMS-compromise, or rogue-HDMI-device categories.

steps.title: Document the unauthorized content and notify on-site staff
steps.desc: Photograph the unauthorized content and alert relevant on-site staff/Facilities.

steps.title: Power off or disconnect the display immediately
steps.desc: Stop the unauthorized content from being visible as quickly as possible.

steps.title: Close the exploited access vector
steps.desc: Address the compromised credential, vulnerability, or physical-security gap identified during identification.

steps.title: Restore approved content and reconnect the display
steps.desc: Confirm the display shows only approved content before reconnecting it for use.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and one concrete improvement, and note whether a more specific ITID category should have been used.

steps.title: Determine whether the cause is remote (CMS/network) or physical (on-site access)
steps.desc: Check relevant CMS/AV system logs and look for signs of physical tampering.
steps.outcome: Access vector — remote or physical — identified.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by powering off the display.

steps.title: Rotate relevant credentials and/or secure physical access
steps.desc: Reset relevant credentials and coordinate with Facilities/Physical Security if physical access may have been involved.
steps.outcome: Old credentials invalidated and/or physical access secured.

ITID-21631.def: Unauthorized alteration of the displayed content, interface, or configuration of a customer-facing self-service check-in or ordering kiosk.
ITID-21631.purpose: Captures tampering with a self-service check-in or ordering kiosk (e.g. hotel check-in, restaurant ordering, event registration) used directly by customers.
scopeIncludes: Defaced kiosk interface/home screen shown to customers
Unauthorized content or menu injected into the ordering/check-in flow
scopeExcludes: Retail point-of-sale terminal tampering, which is scoped separately due to its direct payment-processing context (ITID-21632)
Tampering via physical USB/peripheral access as the differentiating vector (ITID-21633) or via compromised remote management/update channel (ITID-21634)
ITID-21631.severity: Medium-High; direct customer-facing exposure at the point of service.
ITID-21631.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the tampering could mislead customers into an unsafe or fraudulent action (e.g. fake payment step).
ITID-21631.escalation: Escalate to IT security and site/operations management; take the affected kiosk offline pending investigation.
indicators: Customer or staff reports of an unusual kiosk screen
Kiosk management system logs showing unauthorized content/configuration changes
Kiosk behaving outside its documented workflow
vectors: Compromised kiosk management/admin account
Exploited application-layer vulnerability in the kiosk software
rootCauses: Weak access controls on kiosk management systems
Unpatched kiosk application software
controls: MFA on kiosk management/admin accounts
Patch management for kiosk application software
Kiosk-mode lockdown preventing access to the underlying OS
ITID-21631.detection: Kiosk management system logs and on-site staff/customer reports provide the primary detection signal.
ITID-21631.response: Take the kiosk offline, restore the approved interface/configuration, and verify no customer data or payment flow was compromised.
metrics: Time to take the affected kiosk offline
Number of customers who interacted with the tampered kiosk
ITID-21631.notes: Distinguished from POS terminal tampering by its check-in/ordering function rather than direct payment processing; access-vector siblings (USB/peripheral, remote management) carry the underlying-cause detail.

playbook.name: Response: Self-Service Check-In/Ordering Kiosk Tampering
playbook.description: For unauthorized content or behavior on a self-service check-in or ordering kiosk (e.g. hotel check-in, restaurant/retail ordering) facing customers directly.

steps.title: Take the kiosk out of customer-facing service and document the tampering
steps.desc: Remove the affected kiosk from active use and photograph/record the unauthorized content or behavior.
steps.guidance: Customer-facing kiosks often handle payment or personal data — treat with urgency.

steps.title: Keep the kiosk offline and isolate it from the network if remotely compromised
steps.desc: Prevent further customer interaction with the tampered kiosk and isolate it from the network if the software/platform is suspected.
steps.outcome: Kiosk isolated; no further customer exposure.

steps.title: Close the exploited access vector and check for data exposure
steps.desc: Remediate the compromised credential, vulnerability, or physical-tampering point, and check whether any customer data entered during the tampering window was exposed.
steps.outcome: Access vector closed; data-exposure risk assessed.

steps.title: Restore the kiosk to its approved configuration and return to service
steps.desc: Confirm the kiosk is running approved software/content before returning it to customer-facing service.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend a hardening improvement (physical kiosk locks, software patch cadence).

steps.title: Determine whether the cause is remote (kiosk software/CMS) or physical (on-site access)
steps.desc: Check the kiosk management platform's logs and inspect the kiosk itself for signs of physical tampering (forced casing, connected USB device).
steps.outcome: Access vector — remote or physical — identified.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by keeping the kiosk offline.

steps.title: Rotate kiosk management platform credentials
steps.desc: Reset passwords and API keys for accounts with kiosk content/configuration access.

steps.title: Notify affected customers if personal or payment data may have been exposed
steps.desc: Coordinate with Legal and PR/Comms on any required customer notification.

ITID-21632.def: Unauthorized alteration of the displayed content, interface, or configuration of a retail point-of-sale terminal used to process customer payments.
ITID-21632.purpose: Captures tampering with a retail point-of-sale (POS) terminal, distinguished by its direct role in payment processing and elevated PCI-relevant risk.
scopeIncludes: Defaced POS terminal display/interface shown to customers or cashiers
Unauthorized content injected into the POS checkout flow
scopeExcludes: Self-service check-in/ordering kiosk tampering without direct payment-processing involvement (ITID-21631)
Payment-card skimming/data-capture without a visible interface-defacement component (tracked under a payment-fraud ITID elsewhere)
ITID-21632.severity: Critical; direct proximity to payment processing raises PCI-DSS and customer financial-fraud concerns.
ITID-21632.priority: P1, treated with the same urgency as a payment-fraud incident.
ITID-21632.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security, PCI compliance, and store/retail operations; take the affected terminal out of service.
indicators: Cashier or customer reports of an unusual POS screen
POS management system logs showing unauthorized configuration changes
Discrepancy between expected and displayed transaction flow
vectors: Compromised POS management/admin account
Physical tampering with the POS terminal or its peripherals
Malware injected into the POS software stack
rootCauses: Weak access controls on POS management systems
Insufficient physical security around POS terminals
Unpatched POS software
controls: PCI-DSS compliant POS terminal hardening
Physical security controls around POS terminals
POS software patch management
ITID-21632.detection: POS management system logs, PCI-monitoring tools, and staff/customer reports together provide detection coverage.
ITID-21632.response: Take the terminal out of service immediately, verify payment-data integrity was not compromised, and engage PCI incident response procedures if warranted.
metrics: Time to take the terminal out of service
Number of transactions processed during the tampering window
ITID-21632.notes: Reserved for the payment-processing context specifically; treated as the more severe sibling within this Tier-4 group given PCI implications.

playbook.name: Response: Retail Point-of-Sale (POS) Terminal Tampering
playbook.description: For unauthorized content, software, or hardware tampering on a retail point-of-sale terminal, which carries elevated payment-card risk beyond a typical defacement.

steps.title: Take the POS terminal out of service immediately and preserve it for forensic review
steps.desc: Remove the affected terminal from active transaction processing without wiping it, and photograph any unauthorized content or hardware found.
steps.guidance: Given potential card-skimming implications, avoid actions that could destroy forensic evidence.

steps.title: Isolate the terminal from the payment network
steps.desc: Disconnect the terminal from the network/payment processor to prevent further unauthorized transactions or data capture.
steps.outcome: Terminal isolated; no further transaction risk.

steps.title: Remove any skimming hardware or malicious software and close the access vector
steps.desc: Remove any physical skimmer found and remediate the software/configuration vulnerability identified during identification.
steps.outcome: Access vector closed; hardware/software confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore the terminal to service only after verification
steps.desc: Confirm the terminal is running approved software with no residual tampering before returning it to service.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend tamper-evident seals, regular physical inspections, or POS software hardening.

steps.title: Inspect for a physical skimming device and determine the access vector
steps.desc: Physically inspect the terminal for an attached skimmer or tampered card reader, and review POS management/software logs for remote tampering.
steps.guidance: Treat any confirmed skimmer as a payment-card compromise requiring PCI/card-network notification, not just a defacement.
steps.outcome: Physical tampering assessed; access vector identified.
steps.abort: If a skimmer is found, escalate immediately to the payment-security/PCI incident process in parallel with this playbook.

steps.title: Rotate POS management credentials and secure the store location
steps.desc: Reset credentials for the POS management platform and, if physical tampering is suspected, coordinate with Facilities/Physical Security to secure the location.

steps.title: Coordinate customer notification and card-network reporting if payment data was exposed
steps.desc: Work with Legal, PR/Comms, and the payment processor on required notifications if card data was compromised.

ITID-21633.def: Unauthorized alteration of a kiosk or POS terminal's content or configuration achieved by physically connecting an unauthorized USB device or peripheral to the terminal.
ITID-21633.purpose: Captures kiosk/POS tampering achieved through direct physical USB or peripheral access to the device, as the differentiating access vector.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized USB drive or peripheral connected to a kiosk/POS terminal to alter its display or configuration
Physical access to an exposed USB port used to load unauthorized software onto the device
scopeExcludes: Tampering achieved remotely via a compromised management/update channel (ITID-21634)
Tampering with no evidence of physical USB/peripheral involvement (tracked under ITID-21631/21632 as appropriate)
ITID-21633.severity: Medium-High; requires physical proximity, indicating an insider, contractor, or on-site trespasser.
ITID-21633.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the terminal is a payment-processing POS device.
ITID-21633.escalation: Escalate to IT security and physical security jointly; review site access logs/CCTV for the affected terminal's location.
indicators: Unrecognized USB device found connected to a kiosk/POS terminal
Terminal behaving outside its expected software configuration with no remote-management record of the change
CCTV or access-log record of unauthorized physical access to the terminal
vectors: Exposed/unsecured USB ports on kiosk or POS hardware
Insider or contractor with physical access to the terminal
rootCauses: Lack of physical port security (locks/covers/tamper seals) on kiosk/POS hardware
Insufficient site access monitoring around terminals
controls: Physical port locks/tamper-evident seals on kiosk/POS hardware
Site access monitoring/CCTV coverage for terminal locations
ITID-21633.detection: Physical tamper evidence and site CCTV/access logs are the primary detection signal.
ITID-21633.response: Secure the terminal, remove the unauthorized peripheral, restore approved software/configuration, and investigate how physical access was gained.
metrics: Time to detect and remediate physical tampering
Count of physical-access tampering incidents per site per year
ITID-21633.notes: Differentiated from ITID-21634 by the physical, on-site access vector rather than a remote management-channel compromise.

playbook.name: Response: Kiosk Tampering via Physical USB/Peripheral Access
playbook.description: For a kiosk or POS device tampered with via direct physical connection of an unauthorized USB drive or peripheral device.

steps.title: Locate and photograph the rogue USB/peripheral device before removing it
steps.desc: Identify the unauthorized device connected to the kiosk and photograph it in place as evidence before disconnecting.
steps.guidance: This is fundamentally a physical security incident — loop in Facilities/Physical Security immediately.

steps.title: Remove the rogue device and take the kiosk out of service
steps.desc: Disconnect the unauthorized peripheral and stop customer interaction with the kiosk pending investigation.

steps.title: Scan the kiosk for malware potentially introduced via the device
steps.desc: Run a full malware scan on the kiosk given the direct physical connection of an unauthorized device.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or malware found and removed.

steps.title: Restore the kiosk to its approved configuration and return to service
steps.desc: Confirm the kiosk is running approved software before returning it to customer-facing service.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend physical-security hardening
steps.desc: Record how physical access was gained and recommend port security, tamper-evident casing, or camera coverage.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and shared with Facilities/Physical Security.

steps.title: Review physical access logs/CCTV for the area and time window
steps.desc: Determine who had physical access to the kiosk's location during the relevant window.
steps.outcome: Access window and, where possible, the individual(s) responsible identified.
steps.abort: If access cannot be attributed, treat as an unknown-actor physical intrusion and proceed to containment.

steps.title: Disable unused USB/peripheral ports on the kiosk going forward
steps.desc: Where feasible, disable or physically block unused ports to prevent recurrence.

ITID-21634.def: Unauthorized alteration of a kiosk or POS terminal's content or configuration achieved by compromising the remote device-management platform or software-update mechanism used to administer the terminal fleet.
ITID-21634.purpose: Captures kiosk/POS tampering achieved through compromise of the remote management or software-update channel used to administer the device fleet.
scopeIncludes: Compromised remote management platform account used to push unauthorized content/configuration to kiosks or POS terminals
Exploited vulnerability in the software-update mechanism enabling unauthorized code/content delivery
scopeExcludes: Tampering achieved via direct physical USB/peripheral access to a single terminal (ITID-21633)
The underlying vendor/supply-chain vulnerability exploitation as a standalone intrusion without any resulting tampering (tracked under a vulnerability-exploitation ITID elsewhere)
ITID-21634.severity: Critical; remote management-level compromise can affect the entire terminal fleet simultaneously across multiple locations.
ITID-21634.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security and the remote management/POS vendor; consider isolating the management platform from the terminal fleet if compromise is confirmed.
indicators: Remote management platform showing unauthorized configuration or content-push actions
Multiple kiosks/POS terminals affected simultaneously across different locations
Vendor security advisory indicating a platform or update-mechanism compromise
vectors: Compromised remote management platform credential
Exploited vulnerability in the fleet software-update mechanism
Supply-chain compromise of the remote management vendor
rootCauses: Unpatched remote management platform
Lack of MFA on remote management accounts
Insufficient code-signing/integrity verification on pushed software updates
controls: MFA on remote management platform accounts
Code-signing/integrity verification for fleet software updates
Network segmentation between the management platform and terminal fleet
ITID-21634.detection: Remote management platform audit logs and cross-site correlation of simultaneous tampering incidents provide the primary detection signal.
ITID-21634.response: Isolate the remote management platform, rotate credentials, and audit the entire terminal fleet for unauthorized content or software changes.
metrics: Number of terminals affected per incident
Time to isolate the compromised management platform
ITID-21634.notes: Differentiated from ITID-21633 by the remote management-channel access vector rather than direct physical USB/peripheral access.

playbook.name: Response: Kiosk Tampering via Compromised Remote Management/Update Channel
playbook.description: For a kiosk or POS device tampered with via compromise of its remote management or software-update channel, potentially affecting many devices at once.

steps.title: Confirm the remote-management/update channel is the delivery vector and identify all affected devices
steps.desc: Review the remote management platform to confirm the unauthorized content/software was pushed centrally, and identify every kiosk/POS device that received it.
steps.guidance: A compromised update channel can push to every connected device — assume broad impact until scoped.
steps.outcome: Delivery vector confirmed; full scope of affected devices identified.

steps.title: Halt all pending pushes/updates and isolate affected devices from the network
steps.desc: Stop the compromised update channel from reaching any additional devices, and isolate already-affected devices from the network.
steps.outcome: No further devices affected; compromised devices isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malicious update/content from every affected device and close the access vector
steps.desc: Push a clean rollback to all affected devices and remediate the compromised credential or build-pipeline vulnerability.
steps.outcome: All affected devices restored to a clean state; access vector closed.

steps.title: Verify each device individually before returning it to service
steps.desc: Confirm each previously affected kiosk/POS device is running approved software before restoring customer-facing service.
steps.outcome: All devices verified clean and returned to service.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend update-channel hardening
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend code-signing enforcement, MFA on the management platform, or update-approval workflows.

steps.title: Determine how the management/update channel was compromised
steps.desc: Review access logs to determine whether the compromise came from stolen credentials, an exposed management API, or a compromised software-signing/build process.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by halting all pending updates and isolating the management server.

steps.title: Rotate management-platform and update-signing credentials
steps.desc: Reset all credentials and, if applicable, revoke and reissue code-signing keys used for kiosk software updates.

steps.title: Notify affected locations/customers and coordinate with PR/Comms and Legal
steps.desc: Given the multi-device scope, coordinate broader notification with PR/Comms and Legal if customer data may have been affected.

ITID-21635.def: Unauthorized tampering with a self-service kiosk or POS terminal, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (check-in/ordering kiosk, retail POS, physical USB/peripheral access, or compromised remote management channel).
ITID-21635.purpose: Catch-all for kiosk or POS tampering cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to reclassify to a specific kiosk/POS tampering leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-21631 through ITID-21634)
ITID-21635.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as Medium-High pending clarification given potential payment involvement.
ITID-21635.escalation: Reclassify once the specific device type and access vector are clarified.
indicators: Report of tampered kiosk/POS content with unclear device type or vector
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Kiosk/POS physical port lockdown and tamper-evident seals
Application allowlisting/kiosk-mode lockdown on public terminals
Scheduled content and configuration integrity checks
ITID-21635.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-21635.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-21635.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Kiosk or POS Tampering
playbook.description: Catch-all response for kiosk or POS tampering that does not clearly fit the self-service-kiosk, retail-POS, physical-USB-access, or remote-update-channel categories.

steps.title: Take the device out of service and document the tampering
steps.desc: Remove the affected device from active use and photograph/record the unauthorized content or behavior.

steps.title: Keep the device offline and isolate it from the network if remotely compromised
steps.desc: Prevent further customer interaction and isolate from the network if applicable.

steps.title: Close the exploited access vector
steps.desc: Remediate the compromised credential, vulnerability, or physical-tampering point identified during identification.

steps.title: Restore the device to its approved configuration and return to service
steps.desc: Confirm the device is running approved software/content before returning it to service.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector and one concrete improvement, and note whether a more specific ITID category should have been used.

steps.title: Determine whether the cause is remote or physical, and the specific access vector
steps.desc: Check relevant management platform logs and inspect the device for physical tampering.
steps.abort: If the vector can't be determined quickly, proceed to containment by keeping the device offline.

steps.title: Rotate relevant credentials
steps.desc: Reset passwords and API keys for accounts with device management access.

steps.title: Notify affected customers if data exposure is possible
steps.desc: Coordinate with Legal and PR/Comms on any required customer notification.

ITID-21711.def: A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears on both the corporate website and one or more official social media accounts at or near the same time, indicating a linked or shared compromise.
ITID-21711.purpose: Captures coordinated defacement occurring simultaneously across the company website and its social media presence.
scopeIncludes: Simultaneous or closely-timed defacement of the corporate website and a social media account, with evidence linking the two (shared credential, shared attacker, coordinated timing)
A single attacker/campaign responsible for both the website and social media defacement
scopeExcludes: Website defacement alone with no social media component (tracked under the relevant website-defacement ITID elsewhere)
Social media account compromise alone with no website component (tracked under the relevant social-media ITID elsewhere)
Coincidental, unrelated defacements on both channels occurring independently without linkage evidence
ITID-21711.severity: Critical; multi-channel coordination indicates a more capable or determined adversary and multiplies public exposure.
ITID-21711.priority: P1, treated as a major incident requiring cross-functional response.
ITID-21711.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security, social media/communications, and executive leadership; activate the major incident response process given the multi-channel scope.
indicators: Website and social media defacement occurring within a short time window of each other
Same or similar defacement message/imagery appearing on both channels
Shared indicators of compromise (e.g. same source IP, same compromised credential) across both incidents
vectors: Shared/reused administrative credential compromised and used against both the website CMS and the social media account
Single attacker campaign deliberately targeting multiple brand channels for maximum impact
rootCauses: Credential reuse across website CMS and social media management accounts
Lack of cross-channel security monitoring correlation
controls: Prohibition on credential reuse across brand-channel management accounts
Cross-channel security monitoring/correlation for coordinated incidents
Unified incident response playbook covering multi-channel brand attacks
ITID-21711.detection: Requires correlation across website content-integrity monitoring and social media account-activity monitoring; a SIEM/SOAR correlation rule spanning both channels significantly improves detection speed.
ITID-21711.response: Stand up a unified incident response bridging web and social media teams, contain both channels in parallel, and issue a single coordinated public statement.
metrics: Time to detect the cross-channel linkage
Time to full containment across both channels
detections: Cross-channel SIEM correlation rule for simultaneous website/social media content changes
ITID-21711.notes: Requires evidence of linkage between the two channels to qualify for this leaf rather than being logged as two separate single-channel defacement incidents.

playbook.name: Response: Simultaneous Website + Social Media Defacement
playbook.description: For a coordinated attack defacing both the company website and one or more social media accounts at roughly the same time.

steps.title: Designate a single incident commander to coordinate the multi-channel response
steps.desc: Given two distinct channels and teams (web/CMS and social media) are affected simultaneously, name one incident commander to coordinate both workstreams and avoid duplicated or conflicting actions.
steps.outcome: Incident commander named; both workstreams coordinated under one plan.

steps.title: Take the website offline and lock down the social media account(s) in parallel
steps.desc: Simultaneously remove public visibility of both defacements — CDN maintenance page for the site, and password reset/session revocation for social accounts.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer publicly visible on either channel.
steps.tool: CDN / hosting console, social media platform admin

steps.title: Close the access vector(s) and scan for persistence on both channels
steps.desc: Patch the exploited vulnerability and check for any web shell, unauthorized admin account, or scheduled post/automation left behind on either channel.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content on both channels
steps.desc: Restore the website from a known-good backup and delete/replace the defaced social media posts and profile changes.
steps.outcome: Both channels restored to legitimate state.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a cross-channel credential hygiene improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector(s) and recommend improvements such as separating website and social-media credential management, or enforcing MFA on any shared tooling.

steps.title: Capture and preserve the defaced content on both channels
steps.desc: Screenshot and save the website defacement and the social media posts/profile changes before remediation.
steps.outcome: Defaced content preserved on both channels with timestamps.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials shared across or connected to both channels
steps.desc: Reset CMS credentials and social media credentials, including any shared social-media management tool or SSO account implicated.
steps.outcome: Old credentials invalidated across both channels.

steps.title: Coordinate one consistent public statement across both channels with PR/Comms
steps.desc: Since the incident spans two public-facing channels, ensure PR/Comms issues one consistent message rather than separate, potentially conflicting statements.
steps.outcome: Consistent cross-channel public messaging issued if needed.

steps.title: Determine whether both channels share a common access vector
steps.desc: Check whether a single compromised credential (e.g. a shared password manager, SSO account, or social-media management tool also connected to the CMS) explains both defacements.
steps.guidance: A shared root cause changes containment — fixing one channel without the other will not stop the attacker.
steps.outcome: Common or separate access vectors identified.
steps.abort: If a common vector can't be confirmed quickly, contain both channels independently and in parallel.
steps.tool: CMS and social media platform audit logs

ITID-21712.def: A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears on both the corporate website and the company's mobile application at or near the same time, indicating a linked or shared compromise.
ITID-21712.purpose: Captures coordinated defacement occurring simultaneously across the company website and its mobile application.
scopeIncludes: Simultaneous or closely-timed defacement of the corporate website and the mobile app's displayed content (e.g. remotely-configured app banners, CMS-driven in-app content)
A single attacker/campaign responsible for both the website and mobile app defacement
scopeExcludes: Website defacement alone with no mobile app component (tracked under the relevant website-defacement ITID elsewhere)
Mobile app compromise involving malicious code distribution rather than displayed-content defacement (tracked under a mobile app security ITID elsewhere)
ITID-21712.severity: Critical; indicates compromise of a shared backend (e.g. a common CMS/content-delivery service) feeding both channels.
ITID-21712.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security, mobile engineering, and communications; investigate the shared backend/content-delivery service as the likely common point of compromise.
indicators: Website and mobile app displayed content defaced within a short time window
Same or similar defacement content appearing on both channels
Shared backend/CMS or content-delivery service showing unauthorized changes feeding both platforms
vectors: Compromised shared CMS/content-delivery service feeding both the website and mobile app's remote content
Compromised API used by both the website and mobile app to fetch displayed content
rootCauses: Shared backend content service lacking adequate access controls
Insufficient monitoring of the shared content-delivery pipeline
controls: Access controls and monitoring on the shared CMS/content-delivery backend
Content-integrity validation independently on both website and mobile app rendering
ITID-21712.detection: Requires correlation across website content-integrity monitoring and mobile app remote-content monitoring; identifying the shared backend accelerates root-cause detection.
ITID-21712.response: Contain the shared backend/CMS, revert content on both channels, and verify no further shared-service compromise remains.
metrics: Time to identify the shared compromised backend
Time to full containment across both channels
ITID-21712.notes: Requires evidence of linkage (typically a shared backend) between the two channels to qualify for this leaf.

playbook.name: Response: Simultaneous Website + Mobile App Defacement
playbook.description: For a coordinated attack defacing both the company website and its mobile app content/branding at roughly the same time.

steps.title: Designate a single incident commander to coordinate the multi-channel response
steps.desc: Name one incident commander to coordinate the web team and the mobile app team simultaneously, given both channels are affected at once.
steps.outcome: Incident commander named; both workstreams coordinated under one plan.

steps.title: Take the website offline and roll back the app's remote content in parallel
steps.desc: Simultaneously remove public visibility of both defacements — CDN maintenance page for the site, remote-config rollback or forced app-content refresh for the app.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer visible on either channel.

steps.title: Close the access vector(s) and scan for persistence on both channels
steps.desc: Patch the exploited vulnerability and check for any backdoor, unauthorized admin account, or malicious remote-config rule left behind.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content on both channels
steps.desc: Restore the website from a known-good backup and push corrected content/config to the app.
steps.outcome: Both channels restored to legitimate state.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a cross-channel hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector(s) and recommend improvements such as separating web and app content-delivery credentials or adding change-approval on remote-config pushes.

steps.title: Capture and preserve the defaced content on both channels
steps.desc: Screenshot and save the website defacement and the mobile app's altered content (in-app messages, remote-config-driven banners, app store listing if affected).
steps.outcome: Defaced content preserved on both channels with timestamps.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials for the shared or connected backend systems
steps.desc: Reset CMS/remote-config/app-backend credentials implicated in either defacement.
steps.outcome: Old credentials invalidated across both channels.

steps.title: Coordinate one consistent public statement across both channels with PR/Comms
steps.desc: Ensure PR/Comms issues one consistent message covering both the website and app incident rather than separate statements.
steps.outcome: Consistent cross-channel public messaging issued if needed.

steps.title: Determine whether both channels share a common backend/CMS/remote-config source
steps.desc: Mobile app content is often driven by the same CMS or a remote-config service shared with the website — check whether one compromised system explains both defacements.
steps.outcome: Common or separate access vectors identified.
steps.abort: If a common vector can't be confirmed quickly, contain both channels independently and in parallel.

ITID-21713.def: A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears on both an official social media account and an internal platform (e.g. intranet, employee portal, or internal messaging) at or near the same time, indicating a linked compromise spanning both external and internal surfaces.
ITID-21713.purpose: Captures coordinated defacement occurring simultaneously across social media and an internal company platform.
scopeIncludes: Simultaneous or closely-timed defacement of a social media account and an internal platform, with evidence linking the two
A single attacker/campaign using a shared compromised identity (e.g. an employee with both social media and internal-platform access) across both surfaces
scopeExcludes: Social media defacement alone with no internal-platform component (tracked under the relevant social-media ITID elsewhere)
Internal platform defacement alone with no social media component (tracked under the relevant Internal Platform Defacement leaf)
ITID-21713.severity: Critical; the internal/external span suggests a compromised identity with unusually broad reach, or an insider with access to both surfaces.
ITID-21713.priority: P1, with parallel insider-threat assessment given the internal-platform component.
ITID-21713.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security, social media/communications, and insider-threat/HR review given the dual internal-external reach.
indicators: Social media and internal platform defacement occurring within a short time window of each other
Same compromised identity/account exhibiting activity on both the social media and internal platform
Shared indicators of compromise across both incidents
vectors: A single compromised identity (e.g. a social media manager who also has intranet edit rights) exploited across both surfaces
Coordinated attacker campaign deliberately targeting both external and internal brand channels
rootCauses: A single identity holding excessive combined access across both social media management and internal content-editing systems
Lack of cross-surface security monitoring correlation
controls: Least-privilege separation between social media management and internal-platform edit access
Cross-surface security monitoring/correlation for coordinated incidents
Insider-threat review process triggered by cross-surface incidents
ITID-21713.detection: Requires correlation across social media account-activity monitoring and internal platform audit logs; identifying a shared identity accelerates detection.
ITID-21713.response: Contain and revoke the shared compromised/misused identity across both surfaces, revert content on both, and determine whether external compromise or insider action is the root cause.
metrics: Time to identify the shared compromised identity
Time to full containment across both surfaces
ITID-21713.notes: Requires evidence of linkage between the two surfaces; if investigation ultimately confirms a purely malicious-insider motive with no external attacker involvement, cross-reference the relevant ITID-13xxx insider-threat leaf rather than reclassifying away from this leaf, since the defacement act itself remains the primary incident here.

playbook.name: Response: Simultaneous Social Media + Internal Platform Defacement
playbook.description: For a coordinated attack defacing both a public social media account and an internal messaging/collaboration platform at roughly the same time.

steps.title: Designate a single incident commander to coordinate the external and internal response
steps.desc: Name one incident commander to coordinate the external-facing social media response and the internal IT/security response simultaneously.
steps.outcome: Incident commander named; both workstreams coordinated under one plan.

steps.title: Lock down the social media account and the internal platform account/admin access in parallel
steps.desc: Simultaneously secure both channels — password reset and session revocation on social media, and suspension of the compromised internal account with forced logout.
steps.outcome: Attacker access revoked on both channels.
steps.tool: Social media admin / internal messaging platform admin

steps.title: Audit and reverse unauthorized actions on both channels
steps.desc: Review and undo any unauthorized changes made during the compromise window on both the social media account and the internal platform.
steps.outcome: Both channels confirmed clean and restored.
steps.tool: Social media admin / internal messaging platform admin

steps.title: Restore legitimate content on both channels
steps.desc: Restore the social media profile/posts and the internal platform content to their legitimate state.
steps.tool: Social media admin / internal messaging platform admin

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend identity-security hardening
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend MFA enforcement and reduced standing privilege for accounts that span both external and internal platforms.

steps.title: Capture and preserve the defaced content on both channels
steps.desc: Screenshot and save the social media defacement and the internal messaging platform tampering.
steps.outcome: Defaced content preserved on both channels with timestamps.

steps.title: Rotate the shared or connected identity credentials and enforce MFA
steps.desc: Reset the compromised account's credentials at the identity-provider level and enforce MFA before restoring access.

steps.title: Coordinate both a public statement and an internal employee notice
steps.desc: Loop in PR/Comms for the public-facing social media impact and internal communications for the employee-facing platform impact, keeping messaging consistent.
steps.outcome: Consistent public and internal messaging issued if needed.

steps.title: Determine whether both channels share a common compromised identity/SSO account
steps.desc: Check whether a single compromised employee account (especially one with both social-media-management and internal-platform-admin access) explains both incidents.
steps.guidance: This pattern often indicates a broader account or identity-provider compromise, not two unrelated events.
steps.outcome: Common or separate access vectors identified.
steps.abort: If a common vector can't be confirmed quickly, contain both channels independently and in parallel, and treat as a possible identity-provider compromise.

ITID-21714.def: A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears across three or more distinct company channels (any combination of website, social media, mobile app, internal platform, email, or physical displays) at or near the same time.
ITID-21714.purpose: Captures the most severe coordinated defacement scenario, spanning three or more distinct company channels simultaneously.
scopeIncludes: Defacement spanning three or more of: website, social media, mobile app, internal platform, email/messaging, physical digital displays, occurring in a coordinated fashion
Large-scale coordinated brand attacks demonstrating broad access or extensive pre-positioning by the adversary
scopeExcludes: Two-channel coordinated defacement, tracked under the specific two-channel sibling leaf where one exists (ITID-21711, ITID-21712, ITID-21713) or the general coordinated-attack catch-all (ITID-21715)
ITID-21714.severity: Critical; represents the highest-severity defacement scenario in the taxonomy given breadth of impact and implied adversary capability.
ITID-21714.priority: P1, treated as a top-tier major/crisis incident.
ITID-21714.escalation: Escalate immediately to the full incident response leadership team, executive leadership, legal, and communications; activate crisis management procedures.
indicators: Three or more distinct channels showing unauthorized content within a short time window
Consistent defacement message/imagery/threat actor signature across all affected channels
Evidence of extensive pre-positioned access (e.g. multiple compromised credentials or systems) enabling near-simultaneous execution
vectors: Extensive pre-positioned access across multiple systems prior to a coordinated simultaneous execution
Compromise of a shared identity/access-management system granting reach across many channels at once (e.g. a compromised enterprise SSO provider)
rootCauses: Overly centralized access/identity architecture without adequate compartmentalization between channel-management systems
Insufficient cross-channel security monitoring to detect pre-positioning activity before execution
controls: Compartmentalized access architecture separating channel-management systems
Enterprise-wide cross-channel security monitoring and correlation
Crisis management/major incident response plan tested for multi-channel scenarios
ITID-21714.detection: Requires enterprise-wide correlation across all affected channel-monitoring systems; a dedicated cross-channel correlation capability is essential given the scale.
ITID-21714.response: Activate full crisis management response, contain all affected channels in parallel, conduct a comprehensive forensic investigation into the shared root cause, and issue a single coordinated public/stakeholder statement.
metrics: Number of distinct channels affected
Time to full containment across all channels
Time to executive/board notification
ITID-21714.notes: Reserved strictly for three-or-more-channel incidents to keep this leaf distinguishable from the two-channel siblings.

playbook.name: Response: Full-Spectrum Coordinated Defacement (Three or More Channels)
playbook.description: For a coordinated attack defacing three or more distinct company channels simultaneously (e.g. website, social media, mobile app, internal platform, email templates in combination).

steps.title: Stand up a formal incident command structure across all affected channels
steps.desc: Given the breadth of this attack, name a single incident commander with a named owner for each affected channel reporting into them, and establish a shared incident tracker and communication cadence.
steps.guidance: A full-spectrum attack overwhelms ad hoc coordination — treat this as a major incident from the outset.
steps.outcome: Incident command structure established with a channel owner per affected system.

steps.title: Contain every affected channel in parallel
steps.desc: Simultaneously take the website offline, lock down social media, roll back app content, suspend internal platform access, and disable email sends — assign each action to its channel owner to execute at the same time.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer visible on any channel.

steps.title: Close the root-cause access vector and scan every channel for persistence
steps.desc: Remediate the common compromise (or each channel's individual vulnerability) and check every channel for backdoors, unauthorized accounts, or scheduled malicious actions.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content across every channel
steps.desc: Restore each channel to its legitimate, pre-attack state, verifying each independently before declaring it resolved.

steps.title: Conduct a full post-incident review across all channel owners
steps.desc: Document the root cause, the timeline across all channels, and concrete improvements — likely centering on identity/credential architecture given the scale of the attack.
steps.outcome: Comprehensive finding logged and reviewed with leadership.

steps.title: Capture and preserve the defaced content across every affected channel
steps.desc: Screenshot and save the defacement on each channel before any remediation begins.
steps.outcome: Defaced content preserved across all channels with timestamps.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials tied to the identified root cause, or across every channel if no common cause was found
steps.desc: Reset the compromised identity-provider/vault credentials, or reset credentials independently on every affected channel.
steps.outcome: Old credentials invalidated across the environment.

steps.title: Issue one unified public statement and executive briefing coordinated by PR/Comms and Legal
steps.desc: Given the scale of a full-spectrum attack, brief executive leadership and issue a single, unified public statement rather than separate per-channel messages.
steps.outcome: Unified public and executive messaging issued.

steps.title: Determine whether a single common root cause (e.g. identity provider, shared vendor, or password manager) explains the breadth of the attack
steps.desc: Given the number of channels affected simultaneously, prioritize identifying a single common cause (compromised SSO/identity provider, shared credential vault, or shared vendor/platform) over investigating each channel independently.
steps.guidance: A full-spectrum attack is far more likely to stem from one upstream compromise than from independent attacks on each channel.
steps.outcome: Common root cause identified, or channels confirmed to be independently compromised.
steps.abort: If no common cause is found quickly, contain every channel in parallel rather than sequentially.
steps.tool: Identity provider / SSO / credential vault audit logs

ITID-21715.def: A coordinated defacement incident spanning multiple company channels, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (website+social media, website+mobile app, social media+internal platform, or three-or-more-channel full-spectrum attacks).
ITID-21715.purpose: Catch-all for coordinated multi-channel defacement cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to determine exactly which channels are linked and reclassify accordingly
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-21711 through ITID-21714)
ITID-21715.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High pending clarification given the multi-channel nature.
ITID-21715.priority: P1 by default pending reclassification, given the coordinated-attack context.
ITID-21715.escalation: Escalate immediately while clarifying the exact channel scope; do not wait for full clarification before beginning containment.
indicators: Reports of defacement across more than one channel with unclear linkage or full scope
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Centralized credential vaulting across all public-facing channels
Coordinated incident response playbook for multi-channel defacement
Cross-platform account MFA enforcement
ITID-21715.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-21715.response: Begin containment immediately and reclassify to a more specific leaf once the channel scope is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-21715.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one; unlike other catch-all leaves, initial priority is kept high given the coordinated-attack context rather than defaulted low.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Coordinated Multi-Channel Defacement
playbook.description: Catch-all response for a coordinated defacement across multiple channels that does not clearly fit the website+social, website+app, social+internal, or full-spectrum (3+) categories.

steps.title: Designate a single incident commander to coordinate across all affected channels
steps.desc: Name one incident commander to coordinate the response regardless of exactly which channels are involved.
steps.outcome: Incident commander named; workstreams coordinated under one plan.

steps.title: Contain every affected channel in parallel
steps.desc: Simultaneously remove public/internal visibility of the defacement across all affected channels.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer visible on any channel.

steps.title: Close the access vector(s) and scan every channel for persistence
steps.desc: Remediate the compromise and check every affected channel for backdoors or unauthorized changes.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content across every channel
steps.desc: Restore each channel to its legitimate, pre-attack state.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a cross-channel hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the access vector(s) and one concrete improvement, and note whether a more specific ITID category should have been used.

steps.title: Capture and preserve the defaced content across every affected channel
steps.desc: Screenshot and save the defacement on each channel before any remediation begins.
steps.outcome: Defaced content preserved across all channels with timestamps.

steps.title: Rotate all implicated credentials
steps.desc: Reset credentials tied to the common root cause, or independently across every affected channel.

steps.title: Coordinate one consistent public statement across all affected channels with PR/Comms
steps.desc: Ensure messaging is consistent regardless of how many channels were affected.
steps.outcome: Consistent cross-channel messaging issued if needed.

steps.title: Determine whether a common root cause links the affected channels
steps.desc: Check whether a single compromised credential, identity, or shared platform explains the multi-channel pattern.
steps.outcome: Common or separate access vectors identified.
steps.abort: If a common vector can't be confirmed quickly, contain every channel independently and in parallel.

ITID-21721.def: A defacement incident affecting two or more subsidiary brands or business units under the same parent organization, typically via a shared platform, infrastructure, or vendor common to those entities.
ITID-21721.purpose: Captures defacement affecting multiple subsidiaries or brands within the same parent organization, indicating a shared vulnerability or shared infrastructure across the corporate family.
scopeIncludes: Defacement of multiple subsidiary-brand websites/portals sharing common infrastructure or a common CMS instance
A single compromise propagating across sibling brands due to shared credentials or shared administrative access
scopeExcludes: Defacement of a single subsidiary/brand in isolation, tracked under the relevant single-channel ITID
