Cross-brand defacement caused by a shared third-party vendor vulnerability affecting unrelated companies as well as this organization's brands (ITID-21722)
ITID-21721.severity: High; multi-brand impact multiplies reputational exposure and often indicates a systemic shared-infrastructure weakness.
ITID-21721.escalation: Escalate immediately to enterprise IT security and corporate communications; coordinate response across all affected subsidiary/brand teams.
indicators: Defacement appearing on multiple subsidiary/brand-owned properties within a short time window
Shared CMS, hosting, or credential infrastructure identified as the common point of compromise across affected brands
vectors: Compromise of a shared enterprise CMS or hosting platform serving multiple subsidiary brands
Compromised shared administrative credential with access across multiple brand properties
rootCauses: Insufficient segmentation between subsidiary brands' infrastructure and administrative access
Shared credentials used across multiple brand properties without individual accountability
controls: Infrastructure and access segmentation between subsidiary brands
Prohibition on shared administrative credentials across brand properties
Enterprise-wide content-integrity monitoring spanning all subsidiary brands
ITID-21721.detection: Requires enterprise-wide content-integrity monitoring spanning all subsidiary brand properties to detect the cross-brand pattern promptly.
ITID-21721.response: Contain the shared infrastructure/credential compromise, revert content across all affected brands, and implement segmentation improvements to prevent recurrence.
metrics: Number of subsidiary brands affected
Time to full containment across all affected brands
detections: Enterprise-wide content-integrity monitoring across subsidiary brand properties
ITID-21721.notes: Differentiated from ITID-21722 by the shared point of compromise being internal/proprietary corporate-family infrastructure rather than a shared external third-party vendor.

playbook.name: Response: Multi-Subsidiary/Brand Defacement Within Same Parent Organization
playbook.description: For a defacement affecting multiple subsidiary brands under the same parent organization, typically because they share a common platform, credential set, or IT function.

steps.title: Identify every subsidiary/brand affected and designate a single incident commander
steps.desc: Given multiple brands are involved, quickly enumerate every affected property and name one parent-organization incident commander to coordinate across brand teams, which may otherwise operate independently.
steps.outcome: Full list of affected brands identified; incident commander named.

steps.title: Take all affected brand properties offline or to a maintenance page in parallel
steps.desc: Simultaneously prevent further public visibility of the defacement across every affected brand.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer visible on any affected brand property.

steps.title: Close the shared access vector and scan every affected brand for persistence
steps.desc: Patch the shared vulnerability or misconfiguration, and check each affected brand's property for a web shell or unauthorized account.
steps.outcome: All affected brand properties confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content for each affected brand from known-good backups
steps.desc: Restore each brand's property independently, verifying brand-specific content and branding are correct.
steps.outcome: All brand properties restored and verified.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend shared-infrastructure hardening
steps.desc: Record the shared root cause and recommend segmenting credentials/access between brands or hardening the shared platform.

steps.title: Determine the shared infrastructure or credential enabling the cross-brand reach
steps.desc: Identify the common CMS instance, hosting provider, shared IT team credentials, or centralized platform that allowed one compromise to reach multiple brands.
steps.abort: If the shared cause can't be identified quickly, contain each brand's property independently and in parallel.

steps.title: Rotate the shared credentials/access at the parent-organization level
steps.desc: Reset the common credential, API key, or platform access that spans the affected brands.

steps.title: Coordinate one parent-organization statement with per-brand messaging as needed via PR/Comms
steps.desc: Given multiple brands are affected, ensure PR/Comms issues a coordinated response covering the parent organization while allowing brand-appropriate tone per property.
steps.outcome: Consistent, coordinated public messaging issued if needed.

ITID-21722.def: A defacement incident affecting two or more of the company's brands (or the company alongside unrelated external organizations) resulting from a shared vulnerability in a common third-party vendor or platform used across those brands.
ITID-21722.purpose: Captures defacement affecting multiple company brands as a downstream consequence of a shared external vendor or platform vulnerability, often affecting other unrelated organizations as well.
scopeIncludes: Defacement resulting from a widely-exploited vulnerability in a shared third-party CMS, plugin, or platform used by multiple company brands
Mass-defacement campaigns exploiting a shared vendor vulnerability that also affects other, unrelated companies using the same vendor
scopeExcludes: Cross-brand defacement caused by internally shared/proprietary corporate infrastructure rather than a third-party vendor vulnerability (ITID-21721)
ITID-21722.severity: High; the shared-vendor nature usually means the vulnerability is publicly known/actively exploited at scale, requiring urgent patching across all affected brand instances.
ITID-21722.priority: P1, with urgency driven by the likelihood of an active, widely-exploited vulnerability.
ITID-21722.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security and vendor management; check for a vendor security advisory and apply the vendor's patch or mitigation across all affected brand instances without delay.
indicators: Multiple company brands defaced via the same third-party platform/plugin within a short time window
Vendor security advisory or public reporting confirming a mass-exploitation campaign against the shared platform
Other unrelated organizations reporting similar defacement via the same vendor/platform
vectors: Mass exploitation of a known vulnerability in a shared third-party CMS/plugin
Automated/scripted attack campaigns targeting all instances of a vulnerable shared platform
rootCauses: Delayed patching of the shared third-party platform across all brand instances
Lack of centralized visibility into which brands run the vulnerable shared platform
controls: Centralized inventory of shared third-party platforms/plugins across all brands
Expedited emergency-patch process for actively-exploited vendor vulnerabilities
Vendor security advisory monitoring
ITID-21722.detection: Vendor security advisories, public exploitation reporting, and content-integrity monitoring across all brand instances together provide detection coverage.
ITID-21722.response: Apply the vendor's patch/mitigation across every affected brand instance immediately, revert defaced content, and confirm no other unpatched instances remain.
metrics: Time to patch all affected brand instances
Number of brands affected
ITID-21722.notes: Differentiated from ITID-21721 by the shared point of compromise being an external third-party vendor/platform rather than internal corporate-family infrastructure.

playbook.name: Response: Shared Vendor/Platform Vulnerability Cross-Brand Defacement
playbook.description: For a defacement affecting multiple, potentially unrelated brands/organizations because they all use the same third-party vendor or platform with a shared vulnerability.

steps.title: Confirm the shared vendor/platform vulnerability and check public advisories
steps.desc: Identify the common third-party vendor/platform and check for a public vendor advisory or CVE matching the defacement pattern seen elsewhere.
steps.guidance: Cross-organization patterns like this are often reported publicly (security researchers, ISAC bulletins) shortly after they start.
steps.outcome: Vendor/platform and vulnerability confirmed or ruled out.

steps.title: Take the affected property offline or apply the vendor's recommended emergency mitigation
steps.desc: Immediately prevent further public visibility of the defacement, following any emergency mitigation guidance the vendor has published.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer publicly visible.

steps.title: Apply the vendor's patch or fix once available
steps.desc: Update to the patched version or apply the vendor's fix as soon as it is released.
steps.outcome: The shared vulnerability is closed for the company's instance.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content from a known-good backup
steps.desc: Restore the property to its pre-defacement state.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend vendor-risk management improvements
steps.desc: Record the vendor, vulnerability, and recommend faster patch cadence and vendor-advisory monitoring going forward.

steps.title: Determine the company's specific exposure to the vendor vulnerability
steps.desc: Confirm which of the company's properties use the affected vendor/platform version and are therefore at risk.
steps.abort: If exposure can't be scoped quickly, treat every property using the vendor as compromised and contain accordingly.

steps.title: Rotate credentials for the affected vendor/platform account
steps.desc: Reset passwords and API keys for the company's account with the affected vendor.

steps.title: Scan for additional backdoor or persistence
steps.desc: Review the affected property for any web shell or unauthorized account added before the patch was applied.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean, or additional persistence found and removed.

steps.title: Coordinate a public statement with PR/Comms noting the shared, industry-wide nature of the vulnerability
steps.desc: Since other organizations were likely affected by the same vendor issue, a statement acknowledging the shared vendor vulnerability can reduce reputational impact compared to appearing uniquely targeted.

ITID-21723.def: A defacement incident affecting multiple franchise or licensee locations operating under the company's brand, typically via a shared franchise system, template, or vendor common to the franchise network.
ITID-21723.purpose: Captures defacement propagating across a franchise or licensee network, where independently-operated locations share the parent brand identity but operate separate systems.
scopeIncludes: Defacement of multiple franchise/licensee location websites or platforms sharing a common franchise-provided template or system
A single compromise propagating across franchise locations due to a shared franchise-network vendor or system
scopeExcludes: Defacement of the corporate-owned brand properties themselves rather than franchise/licensee-operated properties (tracked under the relevant single-brand ITID)
Cross-brand defacement among wholly-owned subsidiaries rather than independently-operated franchisees (ITID-21721)
ITID-21723.severity: High; franchise-network defacement can rapidly damage brand trust at scale despite the parent company not directly operating the affected systems.
ITID-21723.priority: P1, given the reputational risk despite the operational distance from corporate-owned systems.
ITID-21723.escalation: Escalate to enterprise brand/franchise management and IT security; coordinate with the franchise network's shared-system vendor to contain the propagation.
indicators: Defacement appearing across multiple franchise/licensee locations within a short time window
Franchise-network shared template, CMS, or vendor identified as the common point of compromise
vectors: Compromise of a shared franchise-network CMS or website template provider
Exploited vulnerability in a common franchise point-of-sale or website vendor
rootCauses: Lack of centralized security oversight of independently-operated franchise systems
Franchise agreements not mandating minimum security standards for shared systems
controls: Minimum security standards mandated in franchise agreements for shared systems
Centralized security monitoring visibility into franchise-network shared systems where contractually feasible
ITID-21723.detection: Detection depends heavily on franchise/licensee self-reporting combined with monitoring of the shared franchise-network vendor where visibility exists; coverage is typically weaker than for wholly-owned corporate systems.
ITID-21723.response: Coordinate with the franchise network operator and shared-system vendor to contain and remediate across all affected locations, and communicate guidance to unaffected franchisees to prevent further spread.
metrics: Number of franchise locations affected
Time to coordinate remediation across the franchise network
ITID-21723.notes: Distinguished from ITID-21721 by the franchise/licensee's independent operational status, and from ITID-21722 by the shared point of compromise being a franchise-specific system rather than a broadly-used third-party platform.

playbook.name: Response: Franchise/Licensee Network Cross-Brand Defacement
playbook.description: For a defacement affecting multiple franchisee/licensee-operated sites or properties under the corporate brand, typically due to a shared franchise platform or inconsistent franchisee security practices.

steps.title: Identify every affected franchisee/licensee property and designate an incident commander
steps.desc: Enumerate which franchisee/licensee sites are affected and name one incident commander to coordinate across corporate IT and franchisee operators, who may not have dedicated security staff.
steps.outcome: Affected franchisee properties identified; incident commander named.

steps.title: Take all affected franchisee sites offline or to a maintenance page
steps.desc: Coordinate with corporate IT and/or each franchisee to remove public visibility of the defacement across all affected sites.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer visible on any affected franchisee site.
steps.tool: Franchise platform admin / franchisee IT contacts

steps.title: Close the shared or per-site access vector
steps.desc: Patch the shared franchise platform vulnerability, or work with each affected franchisee to close their individual access vector.
steps.tool: Franchise platform admin / franchisee IT contacts

steps.title: Restore legitimate content across all affected franchisee sites
steps.desc: Restore each affected site from a known-good backup, coordinating with franchisees who may need corporate assistance.
steps.outcome: All affected sites restored and verified.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend franchise-security baseline improvements
steps.desc: Record the root cause and recommend a minimum security baseline or centrally-managed platform for franchisee-operated sites.

steps.title: Determine whether the cause is the shared franchise platform or independent franchisee-level compromises
steps.desc: Check whether all affected sites run the same corporate-provided franchise CMS/template, or whether each franchisee manages its own site independently.
steps.outcome: Shared platform cause identified, or independent franchisee compromises confirmed.
steps.abort: If the cause can't be determined quickly, contain every affected franchisee site in parallel.

steps.title: Rotate shared franchise-platform credentials or notify affected franchisees to rotate their own
steps.desc: Reset shared platform credentials at the corporate level, and direct any independently-managed franchisee sites to rotate their own credentials.
steps.outcome: Old credentials invalidated across affected sites.

steps.title: Coordinate corporate brand messaging with PR/Comms and notify unaffected franchisees to check their own sites
steps.desc: Given the shared corporate brand, ensure consistent messaging and proactively alert other franchisees to verify their own site security.
steps.outcome: Consistent messaging issued; other franchisees alerted.

ITID-21724.def: A defacement incident affecting multiple company brands or affiliated entities, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (multi-subsidiary, shared third-party vendor, or franchise/licensee network).
ITID-21724.purpose: Catch-all for cross-brand defacement cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to determine the specific cross-brand pattern and reclassify accordingly
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-21721 through ITID-21723)
ITID-21724.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High pending clarification given the cross-brand nature.
ITID-21724.priority: P1 by default pending reclassification, given the cross-brand context.
ITID-21724.escalation: Escalate immediately while clarifying the exact affected-brand scope.
indicators: Reports of defacement across more than one brand with unclear linkage or cause
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Shared credential/identity provider review across brand properties
Centralized brand asset access governance
Coordinated incident response playbook for multi-brand incidents
ITID-21724.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-21724.response: Begin containment immediately and reclassify to a more specific leaf once the cause is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-21724.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Cross-Brand Defacement
playbook.description: Catch-all response for a defacement affecting multiple brands/properties that does not clearly fit the multi-subsidiary, shared-vendor-vulnerability, or franchise-network categories.

steps.title: Identify every affected brand/property and designate a single incident commander
steps.desc: Enumerate every affected property and name one incident commander to coordinate the cross-brand response.
steps.outcome: Affected properties identified; incident commander named.

steps.title: Take all affected properties offline or to a maintenance page in parallel
steps.desc: Simultaneously prevent further public visibility of the defacement across every affected property.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer visible anywhere.

steps.title: Close the access vector(s) and scan for persistence
steps.desc: Patch the vulnerability and check every affected property for a web shell or unauthorized account.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content across all affected properties
steps.desc: Restore each property from a known-good backup.

steps.title: Document the incident and recommend a hardening improvement
steps.desc: Record the root cause and one concrete improvement, and note whether a more specific ITID category should have been used.

steps.title: Determine whether a common root cause links the affected brands/properties
steps.desc: Check whether a shared platform, vendor, or credential explains the cross-brand pattern.
steps.outcome: Common or independent root causes identified.
steps.abort: If the cause can't be determined quickly, contain every affected property in parallel.

steps.title: Rotate implicated credentials
steps.desc: Reset credentials tied to the common root cause, or independently across every affected property.

steps.title: Coordinate consistent cross-brand messaging with PR/Comms
steps.desc: Ensure a single coordinated statement covers all affected brands/properties.

ITID-21731.def: An extended defacement campaign characterized by the same channel being defaced again after having already been remediated/reverted, within a relatively short recurrence window.
ITID-21731.purpose: Captures cases where a defaced channel is repeatedly re-defaced after remediation, indicating either incomplete remediation or persistent unaddressed access.
scopeIncludes: A channel defaced, remediated, and then defaced again by the same or an apparently related actor within days to weeks
Repeated re-defacement indicating the original access vector was not fully closed
scopeExcludes: A single, one-time defacement event with no recurrence (tracked under the relevant single-channel ITID)
Long-dwell-time persistent access maintained without repeated visible re-defacement events (ITID-21732)
ITID-21731.severity: High; repeated recurrence indicates a remediation failure and sustained attacker access, elevating both technical and reputational risk.
ITID-21731.priority: P1, given the demonstrated remediation gap.
ITID-21731.escalation: Escalate to senior IT security leadership after the second occurrence; require a full root-cause and access-vector closure review before considering the incident resolved.
indicators: The same page/channel defaced more than once within a short time window
Recurrence despite an initial remediation/revert action
Persistent presence of the same indicators of compromise across occurrences
vectors: Incomplete remediation that reverted content but did not close the original access vector (e.g. credential not rotated, backdoor not removed)
Attacker re-exploiting the same unpatched vulnerability after a content-only revert
rootCauses: Remediation process focused on content reversion without full root-cause/access closure
Lack of a formal post-incident verification step confirming the access vector was actually closed
controls: Mandatory root-cause and access-vector closure verification before closing a defacement incident
Post-remediation monitoring period for affected channels to detect recurrence early
ITID-21731.detection: Content-integrity monitoring on the previously-affected channel, maintained at heightened sensitivity during the post-remediation monitoring period, provides the primary detection signal.
ITID-21731.response: Conduct a full forensic review to identify and close the original access vector (not just revert content again), and maintain heightened monitoring on the channel afterward.
metrics: Number of re-defacement occurrences per incident
Time between remediation and recurrence
ITID-21731.notes: Applies once a channel has been defaced, remediated, and defaced again; the initial single defacement occurrence is tracked under its own channel-specific ITID before recurrence triggers reclassification here.

playbook.name: Response: Repeated Re-Defacement After Remediation
playbook.description: For a website or channel that has been defaced again after a prior remediation, indicating the original fix did not fully address the attacker's access.

steps.title: Review the prior incident's remediation and identify what was missed
steps.desc: Pull the previous incident record and compare what was fixed against what is now being exploited again — the attacker likely retained a foothold the first response did not remove.
steps.guidance: Treat this explicitly as a persistence-hunt, not a routine repeat of the standard defacement playbook.
steps.outcome: Gap in the prior remediation identified, or a genuinely new/independent vector confirmed.

steps.title: Take the site/channel offline immediately
steps.desc: Given this is a repeat incident, prioritize a full takedown over a partial fix while the persistence hunt continues.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer publicly visible.

steps.title: Remove the persistence mechanism and rebuild from a trusted source if needed
steps.desc: Remove the identified backdoor/credential/scheduled task. If confidence in a clean state remains low, rebuild the affected system from a trusted image rather than attempting further incremental cleanup.
steps.outcome: Persistence mechanism removed; environment confirmed trustworthy.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content and monitor closely post-restoration
steps.desc: Restore the site/channel and apply heightened monitoring for a defined period given the repeat nature of the incident.
steps.outcome: Site restored; heightened monitoring in place.

steps.title: Conduct a root-cause review of why the first remediation failed
steps.desc: Document specifically why the original fix did not hold, in addition to the standard incident record, and recommend a change to the remediation-verification process itself.
steps.outcome: Finding logged, including a process improvement for verifying future remediations.

steps.title: Hunt broadly for the persistence mechanism enabling the recurrence
steps.desc: Search comprehensively for an unrevoked compromised credential, a backdoor/web shell missed during the first cleanup, or a scheduled task/cron job re-establishing the defacement.
steps.guidance: Check every admin account, API key, and scheduled job created or modified since before the first incident — not just the ones already suspected.
steps.abort: If persistence cannot be found through log review, consider a full rebuild of the environment from a trusted source rather than continuing to hunt indefinitely.
steps.tool: File integrity monitoring / EDR / audit logs

steps.title: Rotate every credential with any relationship to the affected system, not just the ones used in the original incident
steps.desc: Given the first credential rotation evidently missed something, broaden the scope significantly this time.

steps.title: Independently verify the fix before restoring service
steps.desc: Have someone other than the original responder review the eradication work, given the first fix did not hold.
steps.outcome: Independent confirmation of a clean state.

steps.title: Brief PR/Comms and leadership on the repeat nature of the incident
steps.desc: A second public defacement of the same property carries greater reputational risk than a first-time incident and may warrant a more substantive public response.
steps.outcome: Leadership and PR/Comms briefed; messaging calibrated accordingly.

ITID-21732.def: An extended defacement campaign characterized by an attacker maintaining persistent, long-dwell-time access to a defacement-capable system, discovered well after initial compromise.
ITID-21732.purpose: Captures cases where an attacker maintains long-term persistent access enabling defacement capability over an extended dwell time, whether or not visible defacement occurs continuously.
scopeIncludes: Discovery of a long-standing backdoor or persistent access mechanism in a content-management or display-management system, confirmed capable of enabling defacement
Forensic timeline showing initial compromise significantly predating the visible defacement event(s)
scopeExcludes: Rapid, single-event defacement with no evidence of extended prior dwell time (tracked under the relevant channel-specific ITID)
Repeated re-defacement events without confirmed continuous persistent access between them (ITID-21731)
ITID-21732.severity: Critical; long dwell time implies the attacker may have accessed other systems or data during the same window, beyond just the defacement capability.
ITID-21732.priority: P1, with a full compromise-scope investigation beyond just the defacement channel.
ITID-21732.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security leadership and initiate a broader compromise-assessment engagement given the implied extended access window.
indicators: Forensic evidence of a backdoor, web shell, or persistent credential dating back well before the visible defacement
Log retention gaps or evidence of log tampering consistent with long-term unauthorized access
Confirmation that the same access could have been used for other purposes during the dwell period
vectors: Web shell or backdoor planted during an earlier, undetected compromise
Long-unrotated compromised credential providing persistent standing access
rootCauses: Insufficient log retention/monitoring preventing earlier detection of the initial compromise
Lack of periodic credential rotation and access review on defacement-capable systems
mitreTechniques: T1505.003 Server Software Component: Web Shell
controls: Extended log retention supporting long-dwell-time forensic investigation
Periodic credential rotation and access review on defacement-capable systems
Web shell/backdoor detection tooling on content-management infrastructure
ITID-21732.detection: Requires deep forensic log analysis and web-shell/backdoor detection tooling; standard content-integrity monitoring alone is unlikely to catch this until visible defacement occurs.
ITID-21732.response: Conduct a full compromise assessment covering the entire dwell-time window, remove all persistence mechanisms, and rotate all credentials with access to the affected system.
metrics: Estimated attacker dwell time
Scope of systems/data confirmed or suspected accessed during the dwell period
sops: Digital Forensics and Incident Response SOP
ITID-21732.notes: The confirmed extended dwell time, not just the visible defacement, is the defining characteristic of this leaf; treat as a broader compromise investigation, not solely a content-reversion task.

playbook.name: Response: Long-Dwell-Time Persistent Defacement Access
playbook.description: For a defacement incident where investigation reveals the attacker held access to the affected system for an extended period before the defacement was actually noticed.

steps.title: Establish the true start of attacker access, not just when the defacement was noticed
steps.desc: Review logs as far back as retention allows to establish the earliest evidence of unauthorized access, which may significantly predate the visible defacement.
steps.guidance: A long-dwell-time compromise means the visible defacement is likely the least of the attacker's activity — assume broader access until ruled out.

steps.title: Take the affected system offline and isolate any other systems reached during the dwell period
steps.desc: Contain not just the defaced property but any additional system identified during the dwell-time investigation.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer visible; broader attacker footprint isolated.

steps.title: Conduct a thorough persistence hunt across the full dwell-time scope
steps.desc: Search for backdoors, scheduled tasks, and unauthorized accounts across every system identified in the dwell-time investigation, not just the originally defaced property.
steps.outcome: Full scope confirmed clean, or additional persistence found and removed.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content and systems from backups predating the dwell-time start
steps.desc: Ensure any restoration uses a backup confirmed to predate the true start of attacker access, not just the visible defacement.
steps.outcome: Systems restored from a verified pre-compromise state.

steps.title: Document the dwell-time root cause and recommend detection improvements
steps.desc: Record why the compromise went undetected for so long and recommend monitoring or alerting improvements to reduce future dwell time.
steps.outcome: Finding logged with a specific detection-gap remediation.

steps.title: Investigate what else the attacker may have accessed during the dwell period
steps.desc: Given the extended access window, check for data exfiltration, lateral movement, or other systems the attacker may have reached beyond the defaced property.
steps.outcome: Scope of the attacker's broader activity assessed.
steps.abort: If scope cannot be bounded, escalate to a full incident response investigation rather than treating this as a simple defacement.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials the attacker could plausibly have touched during the dwell period
steps.desc: Given the extended window, rotate credentials broadly rather than narrowly around the defacement itself.

steps.title: Assess and fulfill any data-exposure notification obligations given the extended access window
steps.desc: Coordinate with Legal on whether the dwell-time investigation surfaced any data exposure requiring regulatory or customer notification.
steps.outcome: Required notifications identified and made if applicable.

ITID-21733.def: An extended defacement campaign characterized by multiple distinct stages of escalating scope, severity, or channel reach, carried out deliberately by the same actor or campaign over time.
ITID-21733.purpose: Captures a defacement campaign that escalates in scope or severity across multiple deliberate stages, indicating an adversary iterating toward greater impact.
scopeIncludes: A campaign beginning with a limited/low-severity defacement that escalates to broader or more damaging defacement in subsequent stages
Evidence of deliberate staged escalation (e.g. warning message, then limited defacement, then full-scale multi-channel defacement) attributable to the same actor
scopeExcludes: Repeated re-defacement of the same channel at the same severity level without escalation (ITID-21731)
A single-stage defacement event with no evidence of a deliberate escalation pattern (tracked under the relevant channel-specific ITID)
ITID-21733.severity: Critical; the escalating pattern indicates a determined, iterating adversary likely to continue absent full containment.
ITID-21733.priority: P1, with anticipation of further escalation informing response planning.
ITID-21733.escalation: Escalate to senior IT security and executive leadership at the first sign of an escalating pattern; do not wait for the campaign to reach its most severe stage before treating it as a major incident.
indicators: Sequential defacement events of increasing severity or channel reach attributable to the same actor/campaign
Explicit threat or warning messages within earlier-stage defacements foreshadowing further action
Consistent actor signature/messaging across stages
vectors: Iterative reconnaissance and access expansion between stages, using each stage to probe response effectiveness
Deliberate use of an initial low-severity defacement as a demonstration or warning before broader action
rootCauses: Insufficient containment/root-cause remediation after the initial low-severity stage, allowing the actor to retain and expand access
Underestimation of an early-stage defacement's significance as an escalation precursor
controls: Treating any defacement event as a potential precursor requiring full root-cause investigation, not just content reversion
Threat-intelligence tracking of actor signatures across staged incidents
ITID-21733.detection: Requires cross-incident correlation and actor-attribution analysis to recognize the staged/escalating pattern; individual stages may otherwise be logged as unrelated one-off incidents.
ITID-21733.response: Treat the first-stage defacement with full incident-response rigor to prevent escalation, and correlate any subsequent event against prior incidents to recognize campaign continuity early.
metrics: Number of escalation stages observed
Time between successive stages
ITID-21733.notes: Distinguished from simple re-defacement (ITID-21731) by a deliberate escalation pattern rather than repetition at a constant severity level.

playbook.name: Response: Escalating Multi-Stage Defacement Campaign
playbook.description: For a defacement campaign that escalates over time in scope or severity across multiple stages (e.g. starting as a minor trophy defacement and escalating to malware insertion or broader compromise).

steps.title: Reconstruct the full timeline of the campaign's stages
steps.desc: Document each stage of the campaign observed so far — what changed, when, and how the attacker's objective appears to have evolved.
steps.guidance: An escalating pattern suggests an active, adaptive attacker rather than a one-off event — treat the next stage as likely rather than assuming the campaign has ended.

steps.title: Take the affected system(s) offline and treat the incident at the severity of the highest stage reached so far
steps.desc: Contain based on the worst stage observed, not the current one, given the escalating trend.

steps.title: Conduct a comprehensive persistence and escalation-path hunt
steps.desc: Given the pattern of escalation, search thoroughly for footholds that would enable a further stage — additional backdoors, staged malware, or reconnaissance artifacts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean across the full scope, or additional footholds found and removed.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content and systems from a verified pre-campaign backup
steps.desc: Restore from a backup confirmed to predate the start of the entire campaign, not just its most recent stage.
steps.outcome: Systems restored from a verified pre-compromise state.

steps.title: Document the full campaign and recommend structural improvements to prevent further escalation
steps.desc: Record the complete multi-stage timeline and recommend structural fixes (not just point patches) given the demonstrated pattern of escalation.
steps.outcome: Comprehensive finding logged and reviewed with leadership.

steps.title: Assess likely next-stage escalation and brief the SOC accordingly
steps.desc: Based on the escalation pattern, assess what the attacker may attempt next (e.g. broader access, data exfiltration, ransomware) and put heightened monitoring in place for those specific indicators.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials broadly given the demonstrated escalation
steps.desc: Reset credentials across the full scope implicated by any stage of the campaign, not just the most recent one.

steps.title: Brief leadership and PR/Comms on the escalating nature of the campaign
steps.desc: Given the demonstrated pattern of escalation, ensure leadership understands the risk of further stages and PR/Comms is prepared for a possible follow-up incident.
steps.outcome: Leadership and PR/Comms briefed and prepared.

ITID-21734.def: An extended, multi-event defacement campaign, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (repeated re-defacement, long-dwell-time persistent access, or escalating multi-stage campaign).
ITID-21734.purpose: Catch-all for extended defacement campaign cases that do not fit the more specific leaves under this Type.
scopeIncludes: Cases logged before enough detail is available to determine the specific extended-campaign pattern and reclassify accordingly
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching a more specific sibling ITID (ITID-21731 through ITID-21733)
ITID-21734.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; treat as High pending clarification given the extended-campaign nature.
ITID-21734.escalation: Escalate immediately while clarifying the exact campaign pattern.
indicators: Reports of a multi-event defacement campaign with unclear pattern or cause
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Persistent-access detection and credential rotation following initial compromise
Extended threat hunting for dwell-time indicators
Continuous content-integrity monitoring across campaign duration
ITID-21734.detection: Same general telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-21734.response: Begin containment immediately and reclassify to a more specific leaf once the pattern is confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-21734.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Extended Defacement Campaign
playbook.description: Catch-all response for an extended or repeated defacement campaign that does not clearly fit the repeated-re-defacement, long-dwell-time, or escalating-multi-stage categories.

steps.title: Reconstruct the campaign's history and identify the recurring or extended pattern
steps.desc: Document each known occurrence of the defacement and any pattern in timing, method, or content.

steps.title: Take the affected system(s) offline
steps.desc: Prevent further public visibility of the defacement while the investigation continues.
steps.outcome: Defaced content no longer publicly visible.

steps.title: Remove the persistence mechanism and verify independently before restoring service
steps.desc: Remove any identified backdoor/credential and have someone other than the original responder confirm the fix.
steps.outcome: Persistence mechanism removed and independently verified.

steps.title: Restore legitimate content and apply heightened post-restoration monitoring
steps.desc: Restore the system and monitor closely given the extended/repeated nature of the campaign.
steps.outcome: System restored; heightened monitoring in place.

steps.title: Document the full campaign and recommend structural improvements
steps.desc: Record the complete campaign history and recommend a structural fix, and note whether a more specific ITID category should have been used.

steps.title: Hunt for an unrevoked compromised credential or backdoor explaining the recurrence
steps.desc: Given the extended/repeated nature, search for persistence that earlier responses may have missed.
steps.outcome: Persistence mechanism identified, or ruled out.
steps.abort: If persistence cannot be found through log review, consider a full rebuild of the affected environment.
steps.tool: File integrity monitoring / EDR / audit logs

steps.title: Rotate all relevant credentials broadly
steps.desc: Reset credentials across the full scope implicated by the campaign, not just the most recent incident.

steps.title: Brief PR/Comms and leadership on the extended nature of the campaign
steps.desc: An extended or repeated campaign carries greater reputational risk than a single incident and may warrant a more substantive public response.
steps.outcome: Leadership and PR/Comms briefed; messaging calibrated accordingly.

ITID-22111.def: A fraudulent website that clones or closely imitates a banking, credit union, payment processor, or other financial institution's real site to harvest login credentials, card data, or authorize fraudulent transactions from visitors.
ITID-22111.purpose: Captures a fake website impersonating a banking or financial institution brand used to steal credentials or funds from customers or the public.
scopeIncludes: A cloned or near-identical copy of a bank/financial institution login or payment page
A site harvesting card numbers, account credentials, or one-time passcodes under a financial brand
A fake financial site discovered via customer report, brand-monitoring feed, or takedown vendor
scopeExcludes: Phishing emails or links sent directly to our own employees impersonating a brand (see ITID-11116, ITID-11113 — that variant targets our workforce, not the public)
Credential phishing where the confirmed victim is an internal employee (see ITID-12111)
ITID-22111.severity: High — directly enables financial theft or account takeover against customers/the public.
ITID-22111.priority: P1 while live and actively harvesting; P2 once taken down but still monitored for re-registration.
ITID-22111.escalation: Escalate immediately to brand protection/fraud and legal for takedown; notify affected financial partners if our brand is the specific target of the impersonation.
indicators: Domain/brand-monitoring alert matching our visual identity or trademarks
Customer reports of a suspicious login page
Hosting/registrar pattern consistent with known phishing kit infrastructure
vectors: Cloned HTML/CSS of a real banking portal hosted on freshly registered infrastructure
Distribution via SMS (smishing), search ads, or lookalike domains
rootCauses: Low cost/ease of cloning public-facing web content
Weak or absent proactive domain/brand monitoring
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Brand/domain monitoring service
Rapid takedown process with registrars/hosts
Customer-facing anti-phishing reporting channel
ITID-22111.detection: Primarily external — brand-monitoring feeds, takedown vendor alerts, and customer/public reports; little internal telemetry.
ITID-22111.response: Verify, screenshot/preserve evidence, and initiate takedown within SLA; alert affected customers if credential exposure is suspected.
metrics: Mean time to takedown
Number of confirmed fake banking sites per quarter
ITID-22111.notes: Scoped strictly to sites targeting customers/the public under our brand; phishing that targets our own employees remains under ITID-11xxx (Attacks Against the Human).

playbook.name: Response: Banking/Financial Institution Phishing Website
playbook.description: For a fake website impersonating this organization's banking/financial services to harvest customer credentials.

steps.title: Confirm the site is impersonating this organization
steps.desc: Review the site's branding, URL, and content to confirm it's a genuine impersonation, not a coincidental similarity.
steps.outcome: Confirmed impersonation with evidence captured (screenshots, WHOIS, hosting details).

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a phishing/brand-abuse takedown request to both.
steps.guidance: Include the evidence gathered during identification.

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the hosting provider/registrar action results in the site actually going offline.
steps.guidance: Escalate if no action within a reasonable window.

steps.title: Assist any affected customers who submitted credentials
steps.desc: For any customer known to have entered credentials on the fake site, help them secure their real account.

steps.title: Document the campaign and update brand-monitoring rules
steps.desc: Record the domain pattern/hosting infrastructure used to improve future detection speed.

steps.title: Identify the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the site is hosted and where the domain is registered.

steps.title: Submit the URL to browser/security-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the phishing URL to Google Safe Browsing and major security-vendor threat-intel feeds.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe in major browsers within hours to days.
steps.tool: Google Safe Browsing report / threat-intel submission

steps.title: Warn customers if the site has been actively distributed
steps.desc: If the phishing site was distributed via email/SMS/social to actual customers, issue a warning through official channels.
steps.outcome: Customers warned not to enter credentials on the fake site.

ITID-22112.def: A fraudulent website replicating our organization's actual single sign-on or corporate login page, designed to capture credentials from customers, partners, or the public who mistake it for our real portal.
ITID-22112.purpose: Captures a fake website impersonating our own corporate SSO/login portal to steal customer or partner credentials.
scopeIncludes: A cloned copy of our actual SSO/login page hosted on unauthorized infrastructure
A fake login page harvesting our customer/partner account credentials
scopeExcludes: An SSO phishing page targeting our own internal employees for corporate network access (see ITID-11xxx phishing/credential-theft leaves)
Adversary-in-the-Middle kits targeting internal workforce MFA sessions (see ITID-11114/11124)
ITID-22112.severity: High — direct credential compromise of customer/partner accounts under our brand.
ITID-22112.escalation: Escalate to brand protection and identity/security teams; force password resets for any confirmed harvested accounts.
indicators: Visually identical login page hosted off our infrastructure
Spike in customer-reported suspicious login prompts
vectors: Phishing links distributed via email/SMS pointing to the cloned portal
Search-engine ad placement mimicking our login URL
rootCauses: Absence of visual/DOM fingerprinting to detect clones
No customer-facing domain verification guidance
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Clone-detection/visual fingerprinting service
Customer credential-reset workflow
ITID-22112.detection: External brand-monitoring and customer reports; limited internal telemetry unless harvested credentials are attempted against real portal.
ITID-22112.response: Takedown, credential reset for affected accounts, and customer notification.
metrics: Count of cloned SSO pages detected
Accounts reset due to confirmed harvesting
ITID-22112.notes: Distinct from internal employee-facing SSO phishing/AiTM leaves under ITID-11000, which target our own workforce rather than customers/partners.

playbook.name: Response: SSO/Corporate Login Phishing Website
playbook.description: For a fake website cloning this organization's employee SSO or corporate login page to harvest workforce credentials.

steps.title: Confirm the site clones the real SSO/login portal
steps.desc: Compare the fake page's branding, form fields, and post-submit behavior against the legitimate SSO portal to confirm impersonation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clone with evidence captured (screenshots, source HTML, hosting details).

steps.title: File a takedown request with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit an abuse report citing credential-phishing and trademark/brand impersonation.
steps.guidance: Include screenshots and WHOIS/hosting evidence.

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up with the hosting provider/registrar until the site is confirmed offline.
steps.guidance: Escalate if no action within a reasonable window.

steps.title: Monitor for anomalous logins using potentially compromised credentials
steps.desc: Watch for suspicious authentication attempts against accounts identified as exposed, even after password reset (in case of credential reuse elsewhere).
steps.outcome: No unauthorized access detected, or any detected access is contained.

steps.title: Document the campaign and reinforce phishing awareness training
steps.desc: Record the lure and infrastructure used, and share an example with staff to reinforce recognition of SSO-phishing attempts.
steps.outcome: Finding logged and awareness communication sent.

steps.title: Determine whether any employee credentials were submitted
steps.desc: Check referrer logs, click-tracking on the delivering email/link, or any exfiltration endpoint discovered in the page source for evidence of employee submissions.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the SOC/IAM team.
steps.outcome: List of potentially compromised employee accounts, or confirmation none were affected.

steps.title: Force password reset and MFA re-enrollment for exposed accounts
steps.desc: For any employee identified as having submitted credentials, force an immediate password reset and MFA re-registration.
steps.outcome: Exposed accounts secured before attacker can use captured credentials.

steps.title: Submit the URL to browser and security-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the phishing URL to Google Safe Browsing and relevant threat-intel sharing communities.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe in major browsers.

ITID-22113.def: A fraudulent site posing as a government, tax, or regulatory agency page that references or spoofs our brand (e.g., a fake 'verify your account with [agency] via [our company]' flow) to extract personal or financial data.
ITID-22113.purpose: Captures a fake website impersonating a government or tax agency, using our brand name or association to add legitimacy and defraud the public.
scopeIncludes: Fake tax/government portal pages referencing our brand as the associated business/employer
Sites combining government-agency spoofing with our brand to appear more credible
scopeExcludes: Pure government-agency impersonation with no reference to our brand (outside this taxonomy's brand-protection scope)
W-2/1099 phishing targeting our own employees during tax season (see ITID-51433)
ITID-22113.severity: High — combines regulatory-trust abuse with brand misuse, elevated public-harm potential.
ITID-22113.escalation: Escalate to legal/brand protection and consider coordinated reporting to the impersonated agency.
indicators: Site referencing our company name alongside a government agency's branding
Public/customer reports of a suspicious government-themed page mentioning our company
vectors: Fake tax-refund or benefits-verification pages naming our company as employer/payer
Search ads combining our brand with agency keywords
rootCauses: High public trust in both government agencies and our brand, compounding credibility
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Brand/domain monitoring
Coordinated reporting channel with relevant agency
ITID-22113.detection: External monitoring and public reports only.
ITID-22113.response: Takedown and joint reporting to the impersonated agency where applicable.
metrics: Count of agency+brand combination fake sites detected
ITID-22113.notes: Distinguished from ITID-51433 (W-2/1099 phishing against our own employees), which is an internal-workforce tax-season attack, not a public-facing brand impersonation.

playbook.name: Response: Government/Tax Agency Phishing Website
playbook.description: For a fake website impersonating this organization's tax-document or government-filing related customer service (e.g., a spoofed W-2/1099 or benefits portal) to harvest sensitive personal and tax information.

steps.title: Confirm the site is impersonating this organization's tax/filing service
steps.desc: Review the site's branding, URL, and requested data fields (SSN, tax ID, bank details) to confirm it's impersonating this organization's own tax-related customer service, not a genuine government site.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a takedown request citing phishing and PII/SSN harvesting, which typically receives priority handling.

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the hosting provider/registrar action results in the site going offline.

steps.title: Support customers who submitted SSN/tax data
steps.desc: For any individual known to have submitted sensitive tax data, provide guidance on credit monitoring/identity-theft protection and flag their record for fraud watch.

steps.title: Document the campaign and update seasonal brand-monitoring rules
steps.desc: Record timing (e.g., tax season) and infrastructure patterns to sharpen future detection.

steps.title: Identify the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the site is hosted and where the domain is registered.

steps.title: Submit the URL to browser/security-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the phishing URL to Google Safe Browsing and relevant threat-intel feeds.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe in major browsers.

steps.title: Warn affected customers/employees through official channels
steps.desc: If the site was distributed during a tax-season campaign or targeted a specific population (e.g., payroll customers), issue a warning notice.
steps.outcome: Affected population warned not to enter data on the fake site.

ITID-22114.def: A fraudulent site cloning our streaming/subscription service's sign-in, billing-update, or renewal pages to capture customer payment card data or account credentials.
ITID-22114.purpose: Captures a fake website impersonating a streaming or subscription service brand of ours to steal payment details or credentials.
scopeIncludes: Fake 'update your payment method' or 'renew subscription' pages cloning our service
Fake account-suspension pages prompting credential re-entry
scopeExcludes: Legitimate billing disputes or chargebacks with no impersonation element
ITID-22114.severity: Medium-High — primarily payment-card and low-value account compromise.
ITID-22114.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if a large-scale campaign is confirmed.
ITID-22114.escalation: Escalate to brand protection; notify payment processor if card data harvesting is confirmed.
indicators: Cloned billing-update page under a lookalike domain
Customer reports of unexpected renewal/payment prompts
vectors: Email/SMS campaigns directing customers to fake renewal pages
Search ads for '[our service] billing support'
rootCauses: High volume of routine billing communications makes customers less suspicious of renewal prompts
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Brand/domain monitoring
Customer education on official billing domains
ITID-22114.response: Takedown and customer notification; card reissuance guidance where applicable.
metrics: Count of fake billing/renewal pages detected per quarter
ITID-22114.notes: No internal-employee equivalent exists for this consumer-billing pattern; no cross-domain overlap identified.

playbook.name: Response: Streaming/Subscription Service Phishing Website
playbook.description: For a fake website impersonating this organization's streaming/subscription service login or billing page to harvest customer credentials and payment card details.

steps.title: Confirm the site is impersonating this organization's service
steps.desc: Review the site's branding, URL, and content (e.g., a fake 'billing failed, update your card' page) to confirm impersonation.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a phishing/brand-abuse takedown request to both.

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the site is confirmed offline.

steps.title: Assist customers who submitted payment card details
steps.desc: Advise any customer known to have entered card details on the fake site to contact their bank to cancel/reissue the card, and secure their real account.
steps.outcome: Affected customers' cards and accounts secured.

steps.title: Document the campaign and update brand-monitoring rules
steps.desc: Record the lure pattern and infrastructure used to improve future detection speed.

steps.title: Identify the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the site is hosted and where the domain is registered.

steps.title: Submit the URL to browser/security-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the phishing URL to Google Safe Browsing and relevant threat-intel feeds.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe in major browsers.

steps.title: Warn customers if distributed via email/SMS campaign
steps.desc: If the phishing site was pushed via a mass email/SMS 'your subscription is expiring' lure, issue a customer warning through official channels.
steps.outcome: Customers warned not to enter payment details on the fake site.

ITID-22115.def: A fraudulent website impersonating our brand for phishing purposes, not yet matched to a more specific sector-based leaf (banking, SSO, government, or subscription).
ITID-22115.purpose: Catch-all for fake websites impersonating our brand that do not fit a more specific Phishing Websites leaf.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered fake sites pending classification
Fake sites impersonating sectors not otherwise enumerated (e.g., healthcare, retail loyalty programs)
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching ITID-22111 through ITID-22114
ITID-22115.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; default Medium.
ITID-22115.escalation: Reclassify to a specific leaf once the targeted sector/mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Brand-monitoring alert of unclear sector targeting
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Brand/domain monitoring
ITID-22115.detection: Same external monitoring telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
ITID-22115.response: Investigate and reclassify to a more specific leaf once confirmed.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-22115.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Phishing Website
playbook.description: For a fake website impersonating this organization to harvest customer or employee credentials, where the specific service being spoofed does not fit an existing category.

steps.title: Confirm the site is impersonating this organization
steps.desc: Review the site's branding, URL, and content to confirm genuine impersonation and capture what data it is attempting to harvest.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a phishing/brand-abuse takedown request to both.

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the site is confirmed offline.

steps.title: Assist any affected individuals
steps.desc: For anyone known to have submitted data to the fake site, help them secure any real accounts or credentials that may be reused.

steps.title: Document the campaign and evaluate whether it fits an existing category going forward
steps.desc: Record the site's characteristics; if similar cases recur, consider proposing a dedicated leaf category.

steps.title: Identify the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the site is hosted and where the domain is registered.

steps.title: Submit the URL to browser/security-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the phishing URL to Google Safe Browsing and relevant threat-intel feeds.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe in major browsers.

ITID-22121.def: A fraudulent website posing as an official or unofficial download source for our software, offering 'cracked' or pirated versions bundled with malware, targeting the public rather than our own workforce.
ITID-22121.purpose: Captures a fake site impersonating us to distribute cracked/pirated software or malware disguised as our product downloads.
scopeIncludes: A site offering fake/cracked downloads of our commercial software
Fake 'keygen' or license-bypass tools branded with our product name
scopeExcludes: Malware delivered directly to our own employees via internal phishing (see ITID-31111)
Legitimate open-source or free-tier distribution of our software
ITID-22121.severity: High — malware distributed under our brand can cause reputational and downstream victim harm.
ITID-22121.escalation: Escalate to brand protection and threat intel; coordinate takedown with hosting provider.
indicators: Search results for '[product] crack/keygen' pointing to unauthorized domains
Malware samples referencing our product branding in installer metadata
vectors: SEO-poisoned search results for cracked software
Torrent/file-sharing site listings using our branding
rootCauses: Public demand for free/pirated access to paid software
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Brand/domain monitoring
DMCA/takedown process with search engines and hosts
ITID-22121.detection: External threat intel feeds and malware-sample analysis; limited internal telemetry.
ITID-22121.response: Takedown request, public advisory if campaign is large-scale.
metrics: Count of fake download sites taken down
ITID-22121.notes: Distinct from ITID-31111 (ransomware delivered to us via phishing), which is an attack landing on our own environment rather than the public.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Software Download/Cracked Software Site
playbook.description: For a site distributing malware disguised as this organization's software, or as a 'cracked'/pirated version of it, trading on the brand's name recognition.

steps.title: Confirm the site trades on this organization's brand and distributes malware
steps.desc: Confirm the site references this organization's product name/branding and obtain or safely analyze a sample of the distributed file to confirm malicious content.
steps.guidance: Use an isolated sandbox for any file analysis; never execute on a production or personal device.
steps.outcome: Confirmed brand impersonation and malicious payload, with sample and evidence captured.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a malware-distribution and brand-impersonation takedown request.

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the site is confirmed offline.

steps.title: Support any known-infected users
steps.desc: If any user is confirmed to have downloaded and run the malware, direct them to removal guidance or organizational IT support if it was an employee device.

steps.title: Document the campaign and update brand-monitoring search terms
steps.desc: Record the site's naming pattern and hosting infrastructure to sharpen detection of similar fake-download sites.

steps.title: Identify the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the site is hosted and where the domain is registered.

steps.title: Submit the URL and malware sample to browser/AV-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the URL to Google Safe Browsing and submit the malware sample to major antivirus vendors for signature coverage.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe and malware sample added to AV detection.
steps.tool: Google Safe Browsing report / AV vendor submission portals

steps.title: Warn users if the site is being actively promoted
steps.desc: If the fake download site is ranking in search results or being promoted on forums/social media for this org's software, issue a public warning through official channels.
steps.outcome: Users warned against downloading from the fake site.

ITID-22122.def: A fraudulent site or unofficial listing offering a browser extension/plugin that claims affiliation with our brand, used to deliver malware, adware, or data-harvesting code to end users.
ITID-22122.purpose: Captures a fake site or listing distributing a malicious browser extension impersonating our brand.
scopeIncludes: A malicious extension distributed off official stores claiming to be 'official' for our product
A look-alike extension name/icon combination impersonating ours on a third-party site
scopeExcludes: A legitimate extension of ours that is later found to have a vulnerability (a product security defect, not impersonation)
ITID-22122.severity: High — browser extensions have broad access to user data and sessions.
ITID-22122.escalation: Escalate to brand protection and the relevant browser vendor's extension-abuse reporting channel.
indicators: User/customer reports of a suspicious extension claiming our branding
Extension analysis showing data exfiltration or credential harvesting behavior
vectors: Off-store extension distribution sites
Malicious ads promoting the fake extension
rootCauses: Users seeking convenience features not offered by our official extension
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Brand/domain monitoring
Browser vendor extension-abuse reporting relationship
ITID-22122.detection: External reports and extension-marketplace monitoring; limited internal telemetry.
ITID-22122.response: Report to browser vendor for removal; public advisory if widely distributed.
metrics: Count of malicious extensions reported/removed
ITID-22122.notes: No overlap found with ITID-10000 domain; this pattern has no direct internal-employee equivalent leaf.

playbook.name: Response: Fake Browser Extension/Plugin Distribution Site
playbook.description: For a malicious browser extension or plugin impersonating this organization, distributed outside an official extension store.

steps.title: Confirm the extension impersonates this organization and analyze its behavior
steps.desc: Confirm the extension's branding/name references this organization and review its requested permissions and, where safely possible, its behavior for malicious functionality.
steps.guidance: Analyze in an isolated browser profile/sandbox only.
steps.outcome: Confirmed impersonation and malicious/excessive-permission behavior documented.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a malware-distribution and brand-impersonation takedown request for the distribution page.

steps.title: Confirm the distribution site and/or extension listing are taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the site is offline and, where applicable, the extension is removed from any store.
steps.outcome: Distribution site offline and extension removed/blocked.

steps.title: Advise any known-affected users to remove the extension
steps.desc: For any user confirmed to have installed the malicious extension, provide removal instructions and recommend a credential/session review.

steps.title: Document the campaign and update brand-monitoring for extension impersonation
steps.desc: Record naming/permission patterns to sharpen detection of future fake-extension campaigns.

steps.title: Identify the distribution site's hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the distribution page is hosted and where its domain is registered.

steps.title: Report the extension to the relevant browser vendor(s)
steps.desc: If the extension is also listed in an official store (or sideloaded via a manifest hosted elsewhere), file a malware/impersonation report with the browser vendor (Chrome Web Store, Firefox Add-ons, etc.).
steps.outcome: Extension flagged or removed by the browser vendor.

steps.title: Submit the distribution URL to browser/security-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the URL to Google Safe Browsing and relevant threat-intel feeds.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe in major browsers.

ITID-22123.def: A fraudulent Android/iOS application distributed via sideloading, a third-party app store, or a direct-download link, impersonating our brand's app to deliver malware or harvest data.
ITID-22123.purpose: Captures a fake mobile app distributed outside official app stores, impersonating our brand.
scopeIncludes: APK/IPA files hosted off official stores claiming to be our app
Sideloaded apps using our brand name/icon
scopeExcludes: A malicious app that made it past review onto an official store (typically handled via the app store's own abuse process, tracked separately if we have such a leaf)
ITID-22123.severity: High — mobile malware has broad device access (contacts, SMS, banking apps).
ITID-22123.escalation: Escalate to brand protection and mobile threat intel; coordinate with device/OS vendors where possible.
indicators: Non-official distribution link circulating on forums/social media
Malware sample referencing our brand in app metadata
vectors: Direct APK download links shared via SMS/social media
Fake 'update required' prompts driving sideload installs
rootCauses: Regions/users without easy access to official app stores
Social engineering urging manual installation
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Mobile threat intelligence monitoring
Brand/domain monitoring
ITID-22123.detection: External threat intel and customer reports; limited internal telemetry.
ITID-22123.response: Takedown request to hosting site; public advisory if widespread.
metrics: Count of fake mobile apps identified/taken down

playbook.name: Response: Fake Mobile App Download Site (Non-Store)
playbook.description: For a site distributing a malicious mobile app (APK/IPA sideload) impersonating this organization, outside the official app stores.

steps.title: Confirm the app impersonates this organization and analyze it
steps.desc: Confirm the app's branding/icon/name references this organization and, where safely possible, analyze the package for malicious functionality.
steps.guidance: Analyze only in an isolated mobile sandbox/emulator, never on a production device.
steps.outcome: Confirmed impersonation and malicious behavior documented.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a malware-distribution and brand-impersonation takedown request.

steps.title: Confirm the distribution site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the site is confirmed offline.

steps.title: Advise any known-affected users to remove the app
steps.desc: For any user confirmed to have sideloaded the app, provide removal instructions and recommend a device security scan and credential review.

steps.title: Document the campaign and update brand-monitoring for app impersonation
steps.desc: Record naming/icon patterns and distribution channels to sharpen future detection.

steps.title: Identify the distribution site's hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the download page is hosted and where its domain is registered.

steps.title: Submit the URL and app sample to Google Safe Browsing and mobile security vendors
steps.desc: Report the distribution URL to Google Safe Browsing and submit the app sample to mobile-focused threat-intel/AV vendors (including Google Play Protect) for detection coverage.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe and app sample added to mobile threat detection.
steps.tool: Google Safe Browsing report / Play Protect submission

steps.title: File a trademark/impersonation report if the fake app also appears on a legitimate store listing page
steps.desc: If the sideload page mimics or links from a legitimate app store's branding, report the impersonation to that store's trust and safety team.
steps.outcome: Impersonation reported to the relevant store.

ITID-22124.def: A fraudulent site posing as a media or content-streaming service under our brand, using fake 'watch now' or 'download player' prompts to deliver malware.
ITID-22124.purpose: Captures a malware distribution site disguised as a media/streaming platform impersonating our brand.
scopeIncludes: Fake streaming pages under our brand requiring a 'codec' or 'player' download that is actually malware
Fake live-event streaming pages leveraging our brand name
scopeExcludes: Legitimate third-party syndication of our content under proper licensing
ITID-22124.priority: P2, escalating to P1 during high-traffic events (e.g., a live broadcast) that the site is timed to exploit.
ITID-22124.escalation: Escalate to brand protection immediately if tied to a live event, given the compressed exploitation window.
indicators: Fake streaming domain trending around a scheduled event under our brand
Malware sample disguised as a 'video codec' or 'player update'
vectors: SEO/search-ad poisoning timed to live events
Social media links promising free access to paid content
rootCauses: High public interest in time-limited events creates urgency that suppresses scrutiny
mitreTechniques: T1036.005 Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
controls: Brand/domain monitoring with event-based surge monitoring
ITID-22124.detection: External monitoring only; benefits from proactive registration sweeps ahead of scheduled events.
ITID-22124.response: Rapid takedown, prioritized around live-event timing.
metrics: Count of event-themed fake streaming sites detected

playbook.name: Response: Malware Distribution Site Disguised as Media/Streaming Site
playbook.description: For a site impersonating this organization's media/streaming service to deliver malware, typically via a fake video player, codec installer, or download prompt.

steps.title: Confirm the site impersonates this organization and analyze the delivered payload
steps.desc: Confirm the site's branding references this organization's streaming/media service and, where safely possible, analyze the fake player/codec/download prompt for malicious content.
steps.guidance: Analyze only in an isolated sandbox.
steps.outcome: Confirmed impersonation and malicious payload documented.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the site is confirmed offline.

steps.title: Support any known-infected users
steps.desc: For any user confirmed to have run the fake codec/installer, direct them to removal guidance.

steps.title: Document the campaign and update brand-monitoring rules
steps.desc: Record the site's naming and infrastructure pattern to sharpen future detection.

steps.title: Identify the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Determine where the site is hosted and where the domain is registered.

steps.title: Submit the URL and malware sample to browser/AV-vendor blocklists
steps.desc: Report the URL to Google Safe Browsing and submit the sample to major antivirus vendors.
steps.outcome: URL flagged as unsafe and sample added to AV detection.
steps.tool: Google Safe Browsing report / AV vendor submission

steps.title: Warn users if the site is being actively promoted
steps.desc: If the fake streaming site is ranking in search or spreading via social media/forums, issue a public warning through official channels.
steps.outcome: Users warned against using the fake site.

ITID-22125.def: A fraudulent malware distribution site impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific delivery-mechanism leaf.
ITID-22125.purpose: Catch-all for malware distribution sites impersonating our brand that do not fit a more specific leaf.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered sites pending classification
scopeExcludes: Cases clearly matching ITID-22121 through ITID-22124
ITID-22125.severity: Reassess once more detail is available; default Medium.
ITID-22125.escalation: Reclassify once the specific delivery mechanism is clarified.
indicators: Alert of unclear specific delivery pattern
vectors: Activity of unclear specific vector
rootCauses: Insufficient detail captured at time of detection
controls: Brand/domain monitoring
ITID-22125.detection: Same external telemetry as sibling leaves, pending finer classification.
metrics: Count pending reclassification
ITID-22125.notes: This is an intake/catch-all classification, not a terminal one.

playbook.name: Response: Unclassified / General Malware Distribution Site
playbook.description: For a site impersonating this organization to distribute malware, where the specific lure (software, extension, app, media) does not fit an existing category.

steps.title: Confirm the site impersonates this organization and analyze the payload
steps.desc: Confirm the site's branding references this organization and, where safely possible, analyze the distributed file for malicious content.
steps.guidance: Analyze only in an isolated sandbox.
steps.outcome: Confirmed impersonation and malicious payload documented.

steps.title: File an abuse report with the hosting provider and registrar
steps.desc: Submit a malware-distribution and brand-impersonation takedown request.

steps.title: Confirm the site is taken down
steps.desc: Follow up until the site is confirmed offline.

steps.title: Support any known-infected users
steps.desc: For any user confirmed to have run the malicious file, direct them to removal guidance.
